facts.text: Necrophages are actually post-Conjunction beings that arrived in the world due to the Conjunction of the Spheres.
Vampires are not undead but beings that arrived in the world during the Conjunction of the Spheres.
Relicts are creatures that predate the arrival of men, elves, dwarves, and gnomes into the world, and are often too rare or unique to fit standard taxonomy.

Lara Dorren aep Shiadhal carried an unusually strong line of Hen Ichaer (Elder Blood) and was destined to marry a chosen elf and bear a child able to control the Gates of Time to save the elves from the White Frost.
Natural predators posed an early threat to human settlers, but such predators occupied a normal ecological niche and did not primarily target humans.
After the Conjunction of the Spheres, people used folk magic like scattering salt, nailing silver coins or iron horseshoes, and lighting torches to ward off monsters.
Humans are commonly believed to have arrived in the world alongside the Conjunction of the Spheres, a great magical cataclysm.
The Conjunction of the Spheres is said to have given birth to magic, which then became part of this world.
Ciri is later revealed to carry the Elder Blood, a genetic trait tied to prophecy and immense magical power, and Geralt's survival and role are tied to his destined connection to her.
The Aen Elle believed they were owed a debt from Lara Dorren's betrayal of Ithlinne's prophecy, and wanted Ciri to bear a child with power over the Gate of the Worlds.
Avallac'h believed that only Ciri possessed the power to stop the White Frost, a near-mythical force threatening to destroy not just one world but all worlds.
Witcher neutrality was originally meant to keep witcher schools from becoming political targets of kings or religious authorities.
The Law of Surprise is depicted as a supernatural contract that the universe enforces with absolute rigidity in the Witcher world.
The Nilfgaardian language is based on the Elder Speech, differing completely from the Common Tongue used by the Northern Kingdoms.

The Common Tongue is the language of the Nordling peoples (excluding Skellige) and likely formed from an amalgamation of ancestral languages mixed with local tribal phrases after the first settlement at the mouth of the Yaruga.
The Great Sea forms the western boundary of the known world, and human sailing technology is not yet advanced enough to cross it.
The Dragon Mountains form the northern border of human lands, remaining unexplored due to remoteness and a native dragon population.
The eastern border of the known world is formed by three mountain ranges: the Blue Mountains, the Fiery Mountains, and the Tir Tochair Massif, along with the Korath Desert.
The Blue Mountains contain the source of the Pontar River and the ruins of the elven cities Loc Muinne and Est Haemlet, and are home to the Free Elves who never submitted to human rule.
The Fiery Mountains are the source of the Yaruga River and separate the 'civilized' human lands from the 'barbaric' lands of the East, including Zerrikania and Haakland beyond Elskerdeg Pass.

The area around Elskerdeg Pass is dangerous, home to beasts, wraiths, and tribes hostile to humans; a diary found near a plundered caravan there describes discovering evidence of a cannibalistic feast at an abandoned encampment.
Tir Tochair is the southernmost mountain range forming the eastern boundary of the known world and also forms the eastern frontier of the Nilfgaardian Empire.
Tir Tochair is one of the few remaining enclaves inhabited by gnomes.
Trolls build bridges even in untamed areas like the Kestrel Mountains, hoping to extort tolls from travelers.
The growth of manufacturing, trade, and seafaring directly led to the rise of great port cities such as Novigrad and Pont Vanis.
South of Nilfgaard, rumored lands include Ofir, Zanguebar, Hannu, and Barsa, reached via a marine trade route, though their existence is uncertain.
The land of Barsa is rumored to have a custom requiring all girls to guard their virginity until marriage.

The Northern Kingdoms are a shifting collection of larger and smaller realms that annex neighbors' lands or fragment during civil wars, the four largest and most ambitious being Redania, Kaedwen, Temeria, and Aedirn.
The Skellige Archipelago is one of the earliest lands settled by humans, its people known as skilled sailors, merchants, and pirates who speak a native dialect based on Elder Speech.
Skellige Islanders are predominantly freemen with rights nearly equal to their ruling jarls, unlike mainland Northern societies.
Within the empire, the name 'Nilfgaardian' technically refers only to inhabitants of the original Nilfgaard region, though outsiders use it for all imperial subjects.
Primitive races like ogres, trolls, and half-legendary giants sometimes build settlements in wild, unpopulated regions.
Haakland lies northeast of Zerrikania and its people are rumored to be the world's finest horsemen, learning to ride before they can walk.
The Law of Surprise is a magical phenomenon connecting a person known as the Unexpected Child to someone destined to receive them, typically as payment for a favor.
To invoke the Law of Surprise, the benefactor must agree to give whatever unexpected thing greets them upon returning home, without knowing what that will be.
The Law of Surprise is only finalized if the promised child or person later recognizes the recipient's rightful claim.
A widespread but false belief held that a red cap or hood would protect a young woman from a werewolf, a myth partly spread by the Dyers' Guild for profit.
Witchers are often received with hostility upon arriving in settlements, sometimes facing thrown objects, but friendlier receptions usually mean there is work available.
Sources are individuals with wild, uncontrolled magical talent who act as involuntary conduits for the Power and often have prophetic tendencies.
A source's magical abilities usually remain dormant until they manifest suddenly and violently, often causing destructive, uncontrolled effects.
Trained sources can learn to control and refine their abilities to become powerful sorcerers.
The four Elemental Planes (Fire, Water, Earth, Air) are inhabited by beings called geniuses, each aligned with one element: marides (water), ifrits (fire), d'ao (earth), and djinni (air).
The word 'genie' derives from djinni, the air-aligned geniuses of the Elemental Planes.
Necromancy and demonology (goetia) are forbidden magic disciplines banned by the edicts of the old Conclave due to being dangerous and unethical.
On certain festivities, Prophet Lebioda's bones are taken from his sarcophagus so the pious can kiss them.
Necrophages include ghouls, foglets, rotfiends, and drowners, among other corpse-eating creatures.
Despite their name, most necrophages actively hunt live prey, including humans, rather than only eating carrion.
Some necrophage species bury or store their victims, letting them decay for days or weeks before eating them.
A common but false belief holds that necrophages are humans degenerated by generations of cannibalism.
Because necrophages have no natural ecological niche, killing them does not disrupt the balance of nature, so druids do not object to witchers exterminating them.
Wounds from necrophages carry high risk of tetanus infection and cadaverine contamination.
Necrophages that feed on plague victims can become disease carriers even though they are themselves immune to regular illnesses.
Many necrophages share traits like hairlessness, thin veiny skin, and atrophied sexual organs, suggesting a common post-Conjunction origin.
A folk tale describes a starving hamlet resorting to cannibalism during a harsh winter, eventually giving rise to a tribe that haunts graveyards and battlefields seeking human flesh.
According to folklore, water hags are naiads who fell in love with mortal men, lost their eternal youth, and slowly aged into hags.
Contrary to myth, sunlight is not lethal to most vampires, their bite does not create new vampires, and they are not repelled by garlic or holy water.
Vampires are traditionally split into higher vampires and lesser vampires, a widely used but technically imprecise classification.

Species like alps, mulas, katakans, bruxae, and nekurats are often grouped as higher vampires despite not being true higher vampires; these lesser 'higher vampires' are resistant to sunlight, can disguise themselves as humans, and some can transform or use telepathy.

True higher vampires are an extremely powerful separate breed who nearly perfectly mimic humans, lacking shadows and mirror reflections as their only tell; one such vampire encountered did not trigger a reaction from a witcher medallion.
True higher vampires can turn into giant bats, become invisible, and mesmerize or put victims to sleep with their gaze.
True higher vampires are immune to sunlight, fire, and silver, and can regenerate even from beheading, dismemberment, or incineration, though it may take decades.
The term 'lesser vampires' commonly refers to fleders, ekimmaras, and garkains.
Most ghost stories arise from misidentified natural sounds, but genuine spiritual manifestations do occur as traumatic echoes of violent deaths.
Hybrids are monsters combining traits of two or more creatures, with debated origins either from the Conjunction of the Spheres or predating it.
Creatures called 'the Damned' result from curses, including strigas and botchlings, as well as humans cursed through contact with an original victim, such as werewolves.

A competing theory suggests lycanthropy may be hereditary rather than purely a curse, since some werewolves are born with the trait and can fully control transformation; such werewolves are nearly impossible to cure unless they cooperate willingly.
Draconids are a numerous monster order including at least half a dozen true dragon species plus lesser draconids, long native to the Continent's ecosystem.
Dragons universally love to collect gold, gemstones, and treasure, a trait reflected in countless legends.
Dragon subspecies are classified by color: rock, green, red, black, white, and golden dragons.
Rock dragons are the smallest dragon subspecies and have been hunted to near extinction.
Black dragons are the largest dragon breed, actually a very dark brown color despite their name.
White dragons live in the far North and are known only from tales of a few explorers who describe their scales as light gray or light blue.
The golden dragon, draconis aurum nobilis, is a semimythical creature said to have telepathic communication and shapeshifting abilities, including the power to take human form.

Genies are commonly misnamed lesser elemental creatures summoned from one of four elemental planes (earth, fire, water, air), while true genies are beings of nearly unstoppable power; the lesser elemental servant creatures, though weaker, are still mortally dangerous and can be defeated only by highly skilled individuals.
Trolls have largely abandoned man-eating habits over time and are now considered a primitive intelligent race rather than true monsters.

The prophecy of Ithlinne Aegli aep Aevenien foretold the Time of the Sword and Axe, the White Frost, and the Final Age (Tedd Deireadh), stating the world would perish in ice and be reborn through the Elder Blood, and that first the earth would flow with the blood of the Aen Seidhe, the Blood of Elves.
Ithlinne, the elven seer who made the White Frost prophecy, was known to elves as Zireael, the Swallow, a harbinger of rebirth after the White Frost.
Fisstech is a white powder drug widely used across the Continent, described by City Guard captain Vincent Meiss of Vizima.

Skellige mythology describes an apocalyptic prophecy called Tedd Deireadh, involving the Naglfar ship, the hero Hemdall, and a final conflict called Ragh Nar Roog, in which the Final Age will bring the Time of the White Frost and the Wolf's Blizzard.

Skellige mythology says the cockerel Cambi will crow to herald the arrival of the Naglfar, a longship built from dead men's claws carrying an army of demons from Morhogg, and this crowing will awaken the hero Hemdall, who will stand on the Rainbow Bridge and blow his horn to signal the Last Battle, Ragh nar Roog.
Skellige mythology states the outcome of Ragh nar Roog will determine whether the world falls to Darkness and Cold or whether a new dawn of New Days begins.
Geralt of Rivia was born to Vizenna, a sorceress and druid who was a rare woman able to conceive despite practicing magic.
Ancient dwarven tales claim the gnomes were the oldest inhabitants of the region.
Some scholars believe races such as the vrans or the nearly extinct werebbubbs may also date back many thousands of years.
Dwarves originated in ancient times, even preceding the Conjunction of the Spheres.

Lara Dorren rebelled against her destiny and instead bound her life to a human mage, Cregennan of Lod, bearing his child; both died soon after the child's birth—he killed by elves, she from cold and exhaustion while fleeing pursuers—but their child survived and began the bloodline leading to Cirilla Fiona Elen Riannon.
Vizenna abandoned infant Geralt at the gates of Kaer Morhen, giving him to the witchers of the Wolf School.

Gnomes had small colonies in the mountain regions of Mahakam and Tir Tochair long before dwarves arrived, roughly three to four thousand years before the present, and dwarves arrived in these lands around the same era.

Before humans arrived, ancient races such as vrans, elves, and werebbubbs inhabited the lands that later became witcher territory; as humans expanded, they pushed these races into deep forests and mountains.
Geralt survived the Trial of the Grasses with unusual resilience, leading the mages to subject him to additional experimental mutations.
The extra experimental mutations stripped all pigment from Geralt's body, turning his skin pale and his hair white.
The meeting between gnomes and dwarves was unusually peaceful compared to other racial encounters, and their good relations have continued to the present day.

Some monsters came into the world during the Conjunction of the Spheres, the same event that brought magic into the world, and these post-Conjunction monsters adapted quickly, finding humans, then a weak link in the food chain, easy prey.
Elves arrived roughly two and a half thousand years before the present, landing from white ships, and began a gradual colonization of the region that lasted for about ten centuries.

Elven colonization caused some conflicts with vrans, werebbubbs, and dwarves, though these never escalated into total extermination wars, and relations between elves and dwarves have remained fairly amicable despite past conflicts.

In Blaviken, Geralt was caught between the wizard Stregobor, who believed in a prophecy that girls born during an eclipse become monsters, and Renfri, a cursed princess turned bandit leader Stregobor had long hunted.

Renfri threatened to massacre the market crowd in Blaviken unless Stregobor was forced out of his tower, an ultimatum echoing an earlier 'Tridam Ultimatum' in which her band had killed pilgrims one by one until demands were met.
Geralt attacked and killed Renfri and her gang (seven people total) in the Blaviken market/town square before they could harm anyone, preventing a larger massacre of townsfolk.
The townsfolk of Blaviken did not know about Renfri's ultimatum and instead saw Geralt as a murderous freak, stoning him and driving him out.
The Blaviken massacre, in which Geralt killed six men and a woman in broad daylight in the town market, earned him the lasting reputation and nickname 'Butcher of Blaviken.'
Redania's dynasty traces its roots to the First Landing in the Yaruga delta and was founded by the semi-legendary King Sambuk.
Temeria's history dates back to the First Landing, similar to Redania.
Witchers began using their signature dual blades and medallions several centuries before the game's present day.

According to legend, sorcerer Jan Bekker calmed the ocean's waves during the First Landing by harnessing the Power, commanding the elements to submit to Art, Chaos, and Science; a skeptical academic lecture disputes this, claiming he only harnessed the Power after the Landing and suffered seasickness like everyone else during the crossing.

Individuals with magical talent first began appearing shortly after the Conjunction of the Spheres, mostly as children showing natural magical inclination, and before magic's mechanisms were understood, both sources and other magically touched individuals were ostracized and feared.
The sorcerers' first training seat was the city of Mirthe, known today as Mirt in Redania; Agnes of Glanville, trained there, was the first woman to become a sorceress.

As a young teenager, Emhyr var Emreis was cursed into a half-man, half-hedgehog form by mages working for the man who usurped and murdered his father, the rightful emperor, and he fled to Cintra seeking a cure, as prophecy suggested he might find one there.
Geralt met Dandelion (Julian Alfred Pancratz) at a talent contest in Goulette, where Geralt ended up protecting him from the brothers of a girl Dandelion had seduced.
The Conjunction of the Spheres occurred around one and a half thousand years before the present, according to human reckoning.

The Wozgor and the Dauk were ancient human cultures believed to have arrived directly after the Conjunction of the Spheres, settling lands between the Dragon Mountains and the Gulf of Praxeda; fragmentary information about them mainly comes from remains of their material culture, including menhirs and tombstones.

Proper human expansion into what is now called the Northern Kingdoms began around five hundred years before the present, in an event known as the Landing of the Exiles, when ships made landfall at the Pontar Delta and the mouth of the Yaruga.
It is unknown where the human exiles originally came from, as legends are silent on this detail.

When human exiles first arrived, elves initially avoided armed conflict, hoping the humans would eventually halt their expansion eastward, but elves eventually abandoned some of their cities, which were taken over by human invaders who built structures atop the elven foundations.

No less than two dozen cities of the Northern Kingdoms, including Oxenfurt, Novigrad, Vizima, Maribor, Tretogor, and Cidaris, were built on the sites of ancient elven settlements; the ruins of the elven city Xin'trea are the site of present-day Cintra.
Early human colonists frequently fought among themselves in addition to warring against nonhuman races.
Vrans were eventually pushed into the Blue Mountains, and werebbubbs into remote regions of Mahakam and the Amell Mountains, by expanding human kingdoms.
The southern kingdoms developed independently of the northern ones, and it is unclear if their founders shared ancestry with the northern exiles.

A peace treaty between humans and elves was broken by a treacherous Redanian attack that led to the slaughter at Loc Muinne, sparking the second war between men and elves, in which the flower of elven youth died, a loss from which the elven race never recovered.

Sodden was a former kingdom straddling the Yaruga River; after the First Nordling War and King Ekkehard's death it was divided into Lower Sodden (joining Temeria) and Upper Sodden (joining the Nilfgaardian Province of Cintra); after the Second Nordling War, the Peace of Cintra incorporated Upper Sodden into the Kingdom of Temeria.
Monstrum was widely circulated shortly before the anti-witcher purges that occurred over a century before the game's present.

The school at Mirthe was destroyed during Falka's Rebellion, when the city was burned and its inhabitants massacred; Master Radmir of Tor Carnedd, one of the founders of the magical tradition, was skinned alive on Falka's orders.

About four centuries after the Landing of the Exiles, humans had claimed all lands between the Great Sea and the Blue Mountains, and between the Dragon Mountains and the Amell Mountains, forming the Northern Kingdoms.
Public sentiment turned against witchers over time due to rumors and deliberate incitement, eventually leading to mob violence against witcher strongholds.

After the events in Cintra, Geralt of Rivia continued wandering the world for about ten years before fate intervened again, eventually gaining great fame for lifting the curse on King Foltest's daughter, who had been transformed into a striga terrorizing Vizima.
Geralt of Rivia and Dandelion met Yarpen Zigrin and his gang of dragon hunters, the Crinfrid Reapers, and Geralt refused to let them kill a dragon.
Hallbjorn, a Skellige seaman, recounted that Pavetta and her husband Duny died in a mysterious storm-related maritime accident, which the islanders blamed on the Geas Muire, the Curse of the Sea.

Duny/Emhyr var Emreis plotted with the Cintran army to retake the imperial Nilfgaardian throne while married to Pavetta; a mysterious mage helped him fake his family's death in a staged shipwreck in order to secretly teleport them to Nilfgaard during an uprising meant to place him on the throne.
During a violent argument when Emhyr var Emreis realized Ciri was not aboard, Pavetta fell overboard and died; the mage then teleported the ship to Nilfgaardian land too late to save her.

At Shaerrawedd, roughly two hundred years before the present, the elven leader Aelirenn led a doomed last stand against human forces after most elven leaders had chosen to abandon and destroy their cities instead; her followers fought and died there with no real hope of victory, choosing to die for their symbol and homeland rather than flee.
The account of Aelirenn's last stand was recorded by Cuannah aep Finavail, a comrade of Iorveth and member of the Scoia'tael.

Kaer Morhen fell when a mob, aided by sorcerers' magic, breached its gates and slaughtered nearly everyone inside, including trainees, teaching sorcerers, and witchers; only a few witchers survived because they happened to be away at the time, and the fortress was destroyed probably near the end of the twelfth century.

Nilfgaard was originally a small kingdom that grew into an empire by conquering neighboring lands, later adopting the Great Sun as its emblem, and its power expanded over several centuries until it reached the foothills of the Amell Mountains, bordering the Northern Kingdoms, a few decades before the present.

After the purge, authorities declared the attacks isolated incidents and punished the perpetrators, while survivors speculated the true target had been the sorcerers who trained witchers rather than the witchers themselves.
Following the purge, some witcher laboratories, elixirs, and notes survived, but no one remained who knew how to recreate the mutation and Trial of the Grasses processes.

According to Caldemeyn, ealdorman of Blaviken, seven armed people came to Blaviken including mercenaries Tavik, Nohorn, Fifteen, twins Vyr and Nimir, half-elf bandit Civril, and Renfri (called Shrike).
Geralt and Yennefer of Vengerberg first met in the town of Rinde while Geralt sought a cure for a magical ailment (a throat injury) afflicting Dandelion.
Yennefer was attempting to capture a djinn in Rinde to restore her fertility and increase her magical power.
Geralt used his third and final wish granted by the djinn to magically bind his fate to Yennefer's, saving her from the creature's retaliation.
For six to ten years after the feast in Cintra, Geralt avoided returning to see Ciri, wandering the world and taking contracts in distant lands to escape the responsibility.
Emperor Emhyr var Emreis ordered the invasion of the Northern Kingdoms despite the logistical difficulties of crossing the Amell Mountains and the Yaruga River.
Nilfgaard's first victim in the Northern Wars was the Kingdom of Cintra, whose army was crushed at the Marnadal Stairs a little over a dozen years before the present.
During the Battle of the Marnadal Dale, King Eist Tuirseach was killed, and Queen Calanthe took command, breaking through the Nilfgaardian encirclement to reach Cintra despite grievous wounds.

Cintra's capital fell in an event called the Slaughter of Cintra; the royal castle's remaining defenders chose death over capture, and Queen Calanthe, the Lioness of Cintra, took her own life by leaping from the castle battlements rather than be captured.
During the indolent rule of Vestibor the Proud, Redania lost the fertile Buina and Nimnar valleys to a coalition of northern principalities.

Ten years after the feast in Cintra, Geralt of Rivia visited Calanthe once to formally disavow his rights to Pavetta's child under the Law of Surprise, not wanting to expose the child to witcher training or take them from their family; unbeknownst to him, the child was a girl, and he only learned this years later when he rescued the child from a monster in Brokilon Forest.
After conquering Cintra, Nilfgaard invaded the Kingdom of Sodden, taking Upper Sodden before crossing the Yaruga to attack Northern Sodden.

At the Second Battle of Sodden, a coalition of Redania, Temeria, Aedirn, and Kaedwen under King Vizimir of Redania, aided by Northern sorcerers, halted the Nilfgaardian advance and pushed it back across the Yaruga.
During the Second Battle of Sodden, twenty-two sorcerers made a stand on Kite Hill; thirteen died, and the location was renamed the Hill of Sorcerers or the Hill of the Fourteen.
The First Nilfgaard War ended in a stalemate after the Second Battle of Sodden, with both sides watching each other across the Yaruga.

After the peace following the First Nilfgaard War, the Northern coalition planned a surprise attack to retake Upper Sodden and Cintra, but Emperor Emhyr var Emreis struck first, having had the commanders responsible for the previous defeat executed and replaced with young, ambitious officers loyal to a new 'blitz' style of war.
King Vizimir of Redania, leader of the Northern coalition, was assassinated, plunging his realm into chaos before the Second Northern War.

At the start of the Second Northern War, Scoia'tael units, swayed by promises of elven freedom from Emhyr, attacked the Nordling rear while Nilfgaardian armies crossed the upper Yaruga; Nilfgaardian forces quickly crushed Lyria and Aedirn, while Kaedwen betrayed its allies and switched sides, sealing Aedirn's fate.
King Foltest of Temeria was forced to sign a separate truce with Nilfgaard after King Ervyll of Verden also betrayed the coalition and paid homage to Emhyr.

During the Seven Years' War, Temeria conquered Novigrad, then Redania's capital, forcing Redania to relocate its capital to Tretogor; Radovid III (called 'the Bold' or 'the Red'), grandson of Vestibor, later won back Redania's lost lands and settled the feud with Temeria, resulting in Novigrad becoming a Free City.

Sixteen days after Temeria's truce with Nilfgaard, Nilfgaardian forces, aided by Verden volunteers and Scoia'tael units, attacked Temeria, Brugge, and Lower Sodden anyway; the offensive was halted by winter, and its renewal in spring went poorly due to internal sabotage by opponents of Emhyr.
Queen Meve of Lyria organized resistance forces to harass occupying Nilfgaardian troops, while Verden faced its own anti-imperial uprising.

After the death of King Eist Tuirseach, Skellige islanders became some of Nilfgaard's most determined enemies, launching pirate raids on Nilfgaardian coastal provinces and blockading marine supply lines using their longships alongside the fleet of Ethain of Cidaris.

The Kingdom of Kovir and Poviss officially stayed neutral during the Second Northern War but reportedly gave financial aid to the Northern coalition, and Koviri mercenaries of the Free Company fought on the Northern side.

Geralt of Rivia and Dandelion's first adventure together involved a contract to deal with a devil in the Valley of the Flowers near the Blue Mountains, which turned out to be a sylvan (nicknamed a 'deovel'); during the encounter, elven guerrillas surrounded them, and Geralt's first instinct was to negotiate for Dandelion's safety before his own.
Geralt attended a feast in Cintra hosted by Queen Calanthe under the false identity 'Lord of Ravik' to observe political negotiations over Pavetta's marriage.

A knight/monster known as the Urcheon of Erlenwald, named Duny, with the body of an armored knight and the head of a giant hedgehog, arrived at the Cintra feast and invoked the Law of Surprise to claim Pavetta's hand, having once saved King Roegner's life.
Queen Calanthe intended to have Duny killed to prevent the marriage, but Geralt, recognizing him as a cursed man rather than a true monster, intervened to protect him.

Geralt used his Witcher signs to help break the curse that kept Duny in a beastial form, and the Urcheon of Erlenwald was revealed to be a southern duke named Duny; Queen Calanthe eventually agreed to let him marry Pavetta, restoring his human shape and lifting his curse.
When offered a reward out of gratitude, Geralt invoked the Law of Surprise on Duny as a joking gesture, claiming 'that which you already have but do not know,' entangling him in fate.
At the moment Geralt invoked the Law of Surprise, Pavetta revealed she was already pregnant, meaning Geralt had unknowingly claimed the unborn Ciri (the future Cirilla of Cintra) as his destiny.
Following the fall of Cintra, Ciri became a war refugee wandering the northern kingdoms alone.
Years before the games, Geralt saved Letho of Gulet's life from a manticore/monster, creating a bond of debt and respect between them and earning help from three witchers of the School of the Viper.
The decisive Battle of Brenna saw combined Redanian-Temerian forces, commanded by John Natalis and aided by dwarven volunteers from Mahakam, defeat Nilfgaardian field marshal Menno Coehoorn's army.
Following the Battle of Brenna, the feuding kingdoms of Aedirn and Kaedwen united to defeat Nilfgaardian forces at Aldersberg, ending the Second Northern War.

Kovir was once a remote province of Redania until King Radovid I gave it to his hated brother to keep him away, freeing him from vassal obligations; four generations later, Kovir's mountains were found to contain vast deposits of gold, silver, copper, platinum, iron, and the rare ferroaurum and dimeritium ores.
Archmaster Geoffrey Monck negotiated an agreement at Loc Muinne allowing young sorcerers to learn from elven mages, possibly including the Aen Saevherne.
Prophet Lebioda's cult flourished about one hundred fifty years before the present day, during his own lifetime, gathering a large group of followers who tried to live according to his teachings.
After rescuing Ciri, Geralt of Rivia chose not to take her with him, instead sending her back to Calanthe to be raised under the care of the druid Ermion.
After the Second Northern War, Redania crowned young King Radovid V, who earned the nickname 'the Stern.'
After the Second Northern War, King Foltest of Temeria dealt with Scoia'tael uprisings, the power-grabbing Order of the Flaming Rose led by Jacques de Aldersberg, and rebellious nobles.

Prince Joachim de Wett deliberately underperformed as a Temerian commander due to his involvement in a Nilfgaardian conspiracy against Emperor Emhyr var Emreis; suspecting a conspiracy, Emhyr reassigned him and Duke Ardal aep Dahy to distant command positions in the ongoing Northern War.

A group of Nilfgaardian magnates conspired to remove Emperor Emhyr var Emreis and install the underage Morvran Voorhis on the throne under a regency council, motivated by Emhyr's refusal to marry their daughters.
Emperor Emhyr var Emreis sought to consolidate control over conquered territories by finding Princess Cirilla, the missing heir to the throne of Cintra and granddaughter of Queen Calanthe.
A few years after the Northern Wars, Temeria was riven by internal conflict between oppressed nonhumans and the Order of the Flaming Rose.

Prophet Lebioda died in old age after being set on fire and devoured by a dragon he was trying to exorcise, an exorcism meant to stop the dragon from preying on sheep belonging to Kaedweni villagers; his death was declared a martyrdom, and his recovered bones were placed in a sarcophagus in Novigrad.

Once he secured the Nilfgaardian throne, Emhyr var Emreis declared war on Cintra partly to recover control over his daughter Ciri; before her death, Calanthe managed to get Ciri out of Cintra's capital, causing Emhyr to lose track of his daughter a second time.

Geralt and Ciri were reunited in Sodden after Geralt saved a merchant named Jurgen from monsters and invoked the Law of Surprise again; Jurgen's wife had taken in an orphaned war refugee who turned out to be Ciri.

King Demavend of Aedirn was assassinated, plunging his realm into civil war among burghers, knights, and peasants; about a month later King Foltest of Temeria was also killed, on the eve of his victory over the rebellious House La Valette nobles, leaving Temeria's succession unresolved.

Emperor Emhyr var Emreis manipulated the Lodge of Sorceresses by having his agents pose as their operatives to carry out the assassinations of Demavend and Foltest; the Lodge's own private scheming in Demavend's death was separate but exploited by Emhyr.

The principalities of Creyden, Malleore, Caingorn, and Woefield once formed the East March of Kovir and Poviss before gaining independence during a secession and coup; after two centuries of internal war, King Niedamir of Caingorn united the small principalities into the Hengfors League, named after his capital.
The agreement allowing human-elf magical education was destroyed when Marshall Raupenneck's army massacred the elven population of Est Haemlet and Loc Muinne, sparking another war.

Geralt of Rivia and Dandelion once fished a magic amphora containing an imprisoned genie out of a river; when freed, the genie attacked Dandelion's throat instead of granting wishes. Seeking help for the injury, Geralt traveled to Rinde and met the sorceress Yennefer for the first time.
Yennefer cast a spell on Geralt of Rivia that put him into a trance, causing him to publicly flog several people before fainting and being jailed.

Shortly after Geralt of Rivia returned Ciri to Cintra, the First Nilfgaard War broke out; during the Cintra Massacre, Queen Calanthe died and it was widely believed her granddaughter Ciri had also perished.

At the summit of kings at Loc Muinne, Emperor Emhyr var Emreis revealed the Lodge of Sorceresses' alleged role in the assassinations, using it as a scapegoat and preventing further cooperation between sorcerers and kings; this allowed Nilfgaardian armies to again cross the Yaruga, beginning the Third Northern War, and further weakened both Northern monarchs and mages, clearing the way for renewed invasion.
During the chaos in Rinde, the genie destroyed a quarter of the city before Geralt of Rivia used one of his wishes to win Yennefer's heart and save the city.

Ciri actually survived the Cintra Massacre and found shelter first with druids, then with a peasant family in Riverdell; Geralt of Rivia found her again by chance after saving the life of a farmer who turned out to be sheltering her there.

After reuniting with Ciri, Geralt of Rivia took her to the isolated witcher fortress Kaer Morhen to hide her from Nilfgaard and other schemers, where she trained in swordplay under Geralt, Vesemir, and the other witchers for roughly a year and a half.

Geralt decided to take Ciri to Kaer Morhen, the mountain fortress of the Wolf School, believing it was the safest place for her, breaking Witcher tradition since the fortress had only ever housed Witcher recruits and trainers.
One year into their relationship, Geralt of Rivia left Yennefer's home in Vengerberg without warning, leaving only a letter and a bouquet of violets.
During the journey to Kaer Morhen, Geralt trained Ciri in survival skills such as hiding her trail, sleeping outdoors, and reading forest signs.

During his separation from Yennefer, Geralt of Rivia traveled to the Kingdom of Cintra on a contract that would become the most important of his life, summoned by Queen Calanthe, who feared disruption at her daughter Pavetta's birthday feast.

Geralt of Rivia and his fellow witchers decided Ciri needed a more well-rounded education, so she was sent to Melitele's Temple in Ellander under Mother Nenneke, where she studied history, geography, Elder Speech, and runic calligraphy for over a year.

At Kaer Morhen, Ciri was cared for by Geralt's fellow Witchers Vesemir, Eskel, and Lambert, who acted as father figures and uncles to her, while Geralt personally supervised her training in swordplay and combat techniques.
Ciri was meant to continue her education at Aretuza, the sorceress academy on the Isle of Thanedd, after her year at Ellander.
Geralt of Rivia learned from Northern intelligence about the search for Ciri and decided placing her at Aretuza under Yennefer's care would be safer due to the academy's strong defenses.
The winter Geralt and Ciri spent at Kaer Morhen became a formative period of peace that solidified their father-daughter bond.

Radovid III, called 'the Red,' great-grandson of Radovid I, tried to renegotiate Kovir's independence and marched north with Kaedweni help after King Gedovius of Kovir refused his demands, but the combined Redanian-Kaedweni invasion failed because Kovir used its wealth to hire top mercenary armies to defend its borders.
Since defeating the Redanian-Kaedweni invasion, Kovir has remained neutral and unassaulted, profiting from peaceful trade.

The Rivian/Rivia Pogrom occurred on 25 September 1268, when an altercation—variously described as a tavern argument or a dwarven stallholder's insult to noblewoman and war orphan Nadia Esposita—escalated into a genocidal riot that spread into the Elm district of Rivia.

Geralt was killed/mortally wounded during the Rivian Pogrom when a terrified young man (named Rob), whom he had just spared, stabbed him with a pitchfork while he tried to stop the mob and defend his dwarven and elven friends.
Yennefer arrived after Geralt's mortal wounding in Rivia and exhausted her own life force trying to heal him with magic, nearly killing herself from exhaustion and collapsing over his body.

Kaedwen is the youngest of the Northern Kingdoms, taking its final form two centuries ago during the second war against the elves, and has frequently clashed with neighboring realms, especially Aedirn.
The Novigrad Union was an agreement between sorcerers, priests, and crowned rulers establishing the separation of magic and state for many ages.
The cult of the Eternal Fire began as a local religion limited to Novigrad and its surrounding area; about a century before the present, it was a stern but relatively tolerant faith.
Emhyr var Emreis promised Vilgefortz of Roggeveen control over new provinces carved from the conquered Northern Realms in exchange for his help finding Ciri.
The Peace of Sodden between the North and Nilfgaard was fragile, with both sides waiting for an opportunity to attack the other.

Ciri used her Elder Blood power to transport the bodies of Geralt and Yennefer outside of time and space to the mystical Isle of Avallon, which she had prepared for them, in order to heal them, then vanished from the world herself.

A summit of mages on the Isle of Thanedd, meant to unite magic users, ended in an attempted coup and civil war among mages, known as the Thanedd Coup; Scoia'tael guerrillas fought for the empire's faction while Redanian special forces sided with the other faction.
During the Thanedd Coup, Geralt of Rivia killed several elves and a traitorous mage, and broke the leg of Redanian spymaster Dijkstra.
After being crushed by Vilgefortz of Roggeveen, Geralt of Rivia was rescued by Triss Merigold, who teleported him to Brokilon Forest to recover under the dryads' magic.
After the Thanedd Coup, Yennefer disappeared and was branded a traitor and Vilgefortz's co-conspirator by her fellow sorceresses.
While Geralt and Yennefer were in limbo on Avallon, the Wild Hunt, led by Eredin, tracked Ciri's magical resonance to the island.
The Wild Hunt captured/kidnapped Yennefer on Avallon, intending to use her as bait to lure Ciri out of hiding.

Raffard the White famously arranged peace between kings during the Six Years' War and refused an offered crown, later becoming a royal advisor; the formation of the first Conclave led to a brief civil war in which those who resisted the new hierarchy, including Raffard, were eliminated.
Following the Thanedd Coup, Nilfgaardian troops crossed the Yaruga river and began defeating the Northern allies, gradually seizing their lands.

Geralt of Rivia set out from Brokilon to search for Ciri, initially planning to travel to Nilfgaard itself, and his party traveled through Brugge, Sodden, Riverdell, and Angren while searching for her, seeking guidance from druids in Angren.
While fleeing Vilgefortz during the Thanedd Coup, Ciri stepped into the Tor Lara portal and was transported to the edge of the Korath Desert near the Nilfgaardian Empire's eastern border.
Geralt traded his own soul / offered himself to the Wild Hunt in exchange for Yennefer's freedom, and Eredin took him prisoner instead.

Geralt spent roughly a year serving as one of the spectral red riders of the Wild Hunt, an experience that stripped away his identity and memory, until Ciri devised a plan to rescue him, allowing him to escape back to his world though he lost his memory in the process.
While Geralt served the Wild Hunt, Letho of Gulet and two other Viper witchers protected the amnesiac Yennefer within Nilfgardian territory.

After nearly dying in the Korath Desert and narrowly avoiding Nilfgaardian capture, Ciri was rescued by an outlaw band called the Border Rats, with whom she traveled for several months under the assumed name Falka, earning their respect as a fighter.
Geralt was eventually found near Kaer Morhen with amnesia (described variously as total or partial), remembering nothing of his past, loves, or daughter.
Zoltan Chivay and his band of dwarves parted from Geralt of Rivia's group to return to their homeland of Mahakam.
Geralt of Rivia met the elf Avallac'h, who revealed the secrets of Ciri's ancestry to him.

The bounty hunter Leo Bonhart slaughtered the Border Rats but spared Ciri, recognizing her identity as Falka and intending to collect the bounty on her head, later forcing her to fight as a gladiator in the arena at Claremont for his own amusement.

Geralt of Rivia's group lost Ciri's trail near the autonomous duchy of Toussaint, ruled by Duchess Anna Henrietta, and decided to rest there; while hunting a monster in Toussaint, Geralt overheard information revealing Vilgefortz of Roggeveen's hiding place, prompting him to resume the search for Ciri.
Leo Bonhart planned to hand Ciri over to Vilgefortz of Roggeveen and his ally Stefan Skellen, known as the Tawny Owl, but Ciri escaped, sustaining a wound that left a scar on her face.

Letho of Gulet, acting on orders from the Emperor of Nilfgaard, made a bargain to destabilize the northern kingdoms (using Viper School witchers to assassinate kings) in exchange for restoring/rebuilding the Viper school.

The Aen Elle claimed a debt on Ciri's blood, believing her ancestor Lara Dorren owed them for betraying Ithlinne's prophecy; to return home, Ciri would have needed to give their leader a child with power over the Gate of the Worlds, which the Aen Elle had once before mastered to conquer another world.
Letho of Gulet, acting on orders from the White Flame, assassinated King Demavend of Aedirn and King Foltest of Temeria to destabilize the north.
Letho of Gulet used the Lodge of Sorceresses as a scapegoat to cover his role in the regicides.

Ciri entered a portal at Tor Zireael (the Tower of the Swallow) hoping to reach Thanedd, but instead arrived in the world of the Aen Elle, where she became a pawn in a political conflict between the Sage Avallac'h and Eredin Breacc Glas, leader of the Wild Hunt.
At the end of the second Witcher game, Geralt confronts Letho of Gulet, who calmly explains his motives without asking for forgiveness.
Ciri fled the Aen Elle world using her growing ability to move between worlds, evading Eredin Breacc Glas and his Wild Hunt riders, who chased her but failed to catch her.
The summit at Loc Muinne was held in the ruins of an ancient elven city to address the regicides and reestablish the Conclave of Mages.
The summit at Loc Muinne collapsed into violence when the Lodge of Sorceresses' plot to create a puppet state in the Pontar Valley, ruled by a dragon in human form, was exposed.
After fleeing the Aen Elle, Ciri became lost across unknown times and places before finally arriving at the gates of Stygga Citadel, where Vilgefortz of Roggeveen was hiding.
At Loc Muinne, Geralt fully recovered his lost memories, including the events of Avallon, the Rivian Pogrom, and his bargain with Eredin.
After recovering his memories at Loc Muinne, Geralt learned that Yennefer was alive and held captive in Nilfgard, and that Ciri had returned to the world.
The small Kingdom of Kerack contains little besides the port city of Kerack; its King Viraxas descends from a pirate who declared himself ruler a few generations ago.
Calanthe was known to islanders as the Lioness of Cintra, and her death along with Duny and Pavetta's was mourned as a family tragedy by the people of the Skellige Isles.
The collapse of the Loc Muinne summit triggered the start of the Third Northern War.

When Ciri confronted Vilgefortz at Stygga Citadel, Geralt and his companions arrived to aid her, and Yennefer escaped captivity to join them; the Battle of Stygga Citadel ended with Vilgefortz's defeat and death at Geralt's hands, though Milva, Cahir, Regis, and Angouleme died in the fighting.

After the Battle of Stygga Citadel, Emperor Emhyr var Emreis arrived with imperial soldiers, having learned of Vilgefortz's treachery and his collusion with Stefan Skellen, but unexpectedly showed mercy and let Geralt, Yennefer, and Ciri leave unharmed after looking at his daughter Ciri's face.

Professor Emmerich Gottshalk recorded that the Rivia Pogrom killed almost two hundred people (184 in the hour before Triss Merigold intervened), mostly nonhumans and including many women and children.
In White Orchard, Geralt is accompanied by his mentor Vesemir while searching for leads on Yennefer and Ciri.
To gain information from the Nilfgardian commander in White Orchard, Geralt was forced to kill a griffin threatening supply lines.
Geralt's search for Ciri in The Witcher 3 leads him through three major regions: Velen, Novigrad, and Skellige.
In Velen, Geralt found evidence that Ciri had been a refugee fleeing something more dangerous than the Nilfgardian army.
In Novigrad, Geralt tracked Ciri's movements through the criminal underworld and religious authorities, finding she had matured into a resourceful, powerful woman.
After the Rivia Pogrom, the Wild Hunt led by Eredin continued searching for Ciri; Geralt and Yennefer took refuge on the Isle of Avalon, which Ciri had prepared for them.
In Skellige, Geralt found evidence of a magical explosion and battle linked to Ciri's flight from the Wild Hunt.
Geralt pursued the Wild Hunt across many worlds while searching for the kidnapped Yennefer.
Geralt met with Emperor Emhyr var Emreis, the White Flame, in occupied Vizima, who hired him to find Ciri.
Yennefer allied herself with the Nilfgardian Empire's intelligence network to help locate Ciri.

In Velen, Geralt encountered Philip Strenger, known as the Bloody Baron, who offered information on Ciri in exchange for help finding his missing wife and daughter, and who later recommended she seek help in Novigrad.

The balance of power between sorcerers and rulers shifted after the Second Battle of Sodden during the First Nilfgaard War, when sorcerers' sacrifice helped win the battle, and afterward sorcerers gained influence with kings, some beginning to act as advisors and gain political power.
Several years after the Rivia Pogrom, Geralt reappeared near Kaer Morhen, alive but with amnesia.

Ciri devised a plan to rescue Geralt from the Wild Hunt, allowing him to escape back to his world, though he lost his memory in the process; he found shelter at Kaer Morhen with his Wolf School companions, but Triss Merigold's magic could not restore his lost memory.

Azar Javed, a renegade mage, and an assassin known as the Professor led a surprise attack on Kaer Morhen, stealing secrets of witcher mutations from the keep's laboratory; a witcher died defending Kaer Morhen during the attack.

Geralt traveled to Vizima, capital of Temeria, seeking King Foltest, who was absent from the city; during Foltest's absence, Jacques de Aldersberg, grandmaster of the Order of the Flaming Rose, increased persecution of nonhumans in Vizima, driving elves and dwarves to join local Scoia'tael bands.

Geralt discovered that the Salamandra, a criminal syndicate dealing in fisstech, extortion, and contract killings, was behind the Kaer Morhen attack, and destroyed its fisstech labs and killed its members, working up to the leadership.
Geralt killed the Professor in revenge for the witcher slain at Kaer Morhen.

Geralt confronted and eventually killed Azar Javed, who revealed Jacques de Aldersberg as the mastermind behind the plot to breed mutants using stolen witcher secrets to suppress the nonhuman riots he had incited.

Jacques de Aldersberg trapped Geralt in a magical illusion depicting the frozen world after the apocalyptic White Frost, but Geralt refused his offer to join him and killed him with a witcher's blade.
After Jacques de Aldersberg's death, an assassin who turned out to be a mutated witcher attempted to kill King Foltest, but Geralt stopped the attack, and Foltest made Geralt his personal bodyguard.
King Demavend of Aedirn was assassinated, and about a month later King Foltest was also killed; Geralt was falsely accused of murdering Foltest and imprisoned, but escaped to find the real assassin.

Geralt traveled to the border town of Flotsam and discovered the assassin was Letho of Gulet, a witcher and former companion he no longer remembered; Letho fled by forcing Triss Merigold to teleport them both to the Kingdom of Aedirn.
During the second war with Nilfgaard, Geralt fought at a bridge over the Yaruga River to protect the forces of Queen Meve of Lyria and Rivia.
Queen Meve knighted Geralt for his bravery at the Yaruga River battle, making his invented title 'of Rivia' officially legitimate.
Dandelion once crossed into Brokilon to bring urgent news to his friend Geralt, who was being healed there after being gravely wounded; he survived by charming the dryads with his musical Art.
In Aedirn, Geralt encountered Saskia, the Virgin of Aedirn, leading an uprising amid conflict with King Henselt of Kaedwen, who had seized Aedirnian territory after King Demavend's death.

Geralt discovered that two more Viper School witchers, confederates of Letho, were active in the Aedirn conflict; Geralt fought them and the three Viper School witchers settled their differences with blades.
Before dying, the Viper witchers revealed that Sile de Tansarville of the Lodge of Sorceresses had hired them to kill King Demavend.
Suspected mages and nonhumans were burned publicly in Novigrad's Hierarch Square.

The trails of Sile de Tansarville and Letho of Gulet led to the ancient ruins of Loc Muinne, site of a summit of Northern kings and sorceresses including delegates from Kaedwen, Aedirn, Temeria, and Redania, along with Nilfgaardian observers, aimed at resolving the Temerian succession and considering reactivating the Conclave and Supreme Council of Sorcerers.
The Loc Muinne summit collapsed after Nilfgaardian intervention and was ended by a dragon attack.
During his conversation with Letho, Geralt learned that Yennefer was likely alive in the Nilfgaardian Empire.
Geralt travels to Novigrad searching for Dandelion, the last person known to have seen Ciri in the city.
Geralt performs tasks for the Novigrad crime lords while searching for information about Dandelion and Ciri.
Geralt discovers that Dandelion and Ciri had attempted to rob Dijkstra's vault to fund a way to break a curse affecting Avallac'h.
Taking advantage of the Temerian interregnum and Northern discord, the Nilfgaardian army crossed the Yaruga river to invade the North again.
Geralt helps Triss Merigold organize a mass escape of mages and alchemists through Novigrad's sewers.

Yennefer sent Geralt a letter requesting a meeting in the former Temerian town of Willoughby; while traveling through occupied Temeria, Geralt reunited with his mentor Vesemir, but Willoughby had been destroyed in fighting between Northern armies and Nilfgaard, and Yennefer was not there when they arrived.

Geralt rescues Dandelion after a series of dangerous schemes, including staging a play and a prison break; Dandelion had been captured by guards of the Church of the Eternal Fire and imprisoned after covering Ciri's escape.
Dandelion tells Geralt that Ciri escaped the Temple Guard in Novigrad by teleporting away, going into hiding once more.

Geralt found Yennefer in the village of White Orchard after dealing with a griffin menacing locals and Nilfgaardian troops; she was accompanied by Nilfgaardian guards who told Geralt that Emperor Emhyr needed to see them both.
Geralt and Yennefer were ambushed by the Wild Hunt while traveling to meet Emperor Emhyr in Vizima.
After Novigrad, Geralt heads to the Skellige Isles, believing it to be one of the few places the Eternal Fire's influence has not reached.
Skellige is undergoing a succession crisis following the death of King Bran.
Geralt helps Crach an Craite's children, Hjalmar and Cerys, in their quests connected to the succession crisis, and later becomes involved in choosing Skellige's next ruler between them.

Under the Eternal Fire's growing power, false accusations, show trials, executions, and property confiscation became common, and fear of black magic evolved into hatred of all sorcery, nonhumans, and sorcerers, culminating in witch hunts that killed hundreds of innocents.

Emperor Emhyr revealed that Ciri had returned to their world and asked Geralt to find her, offering gold though Geralt needed no incentive; Emhyr and Yennefer had already been searching for Ciri but stopped after their efforts attracted the Wild Hunt.

Geralt investigates the site of a massive magical explosion on the island of Ard Skellig, caused by a battle between Ciri, Avallac'h, and the Wild Hunt; the vision reveals that Ciri's elder blood power leveled entire forests during the confrontation.
The Wild Hunt's spectral riders attack the village of Undvik, leaving it in ruins and its people haunted.

Ciri's presence was tracked through the war-torn region of Velen, the Free City of Novigrad, and the Skellige Islands; she first arrived back in this world in Skellige, causing a magical explosion that devastated part of the islands.
Ciri fled to Velen, where she encountered the Crones, three demonic sisters, before finding shelter with the Bloody Baron, who recommended she seek help in Novigrad.
Geralt realizes Uma is the key to finding Ciri and travels to Kaer Morhen to attempt to break the curse.
In Novigrad, Ciri sought help from Dandelion to lift a curse; he was captured by guards of the Church of the Eternal Fire and imprisoned after covering her escape.
Geralt and Zoltan Chivay devised a plan to rescue Dandelion from imprisonment.
Following this revelation, Geralt sails to the Isle of Mists to find Ciri.

The Thanedd Coup occurred on the first of July during the Year of the Great War at Garstang Palace on Thanedd Island; roughly two hundred practitioners of magic gathered there, including members of the Conclave and Supreme Council of Sorcerers.

Sorcerers loyal to the Northern Kingdoms at Thanedd included Philippa Eilhart of Redania, Triss Merigold and Keira Metz of Temeria, Radcliffe of Oxenfurt, and Sabrina Glevissig of Kaedwen; they attempted to arrest traitors Vilgefortz of Roggeveen, Artaud Terranova, and Fercart of Cidaris with help from the Redanian Secret Service.
Tissaia de Vries liquidated the barrier spell preventing magic use at Thanedd, allowing conspirators to summon help and triggering an all-out battle.
The traitors at Thanedd were preparing their own coup with help from a hidden unit of Scoia'tael in Garstang's cellars, and sought to capture Cirilla of Cintra.

On the Isle of Mists, Geralt finds Ciri in a catatonic state, her soul seemingly lost after her last interdimensional jump; she is revived through the residual magic of the Will-o'-the-Wisp, waking to see Geralt.

The Thanedd Coup resulted in a massacre killing many sorcerers, with only a handful of traitors escaping, permanently damaging sorcerers' reputation in the North; the Conclave and Supreme Council of Sorcerers were subsequently dissolved, and even loyal sorcerers lost their rulers' trust.
During a clash with the Wild Hunt, Avallac'h was cursed, deforming his body and mind; Geralt, with Yennefer's help, lifted the curse afflicting him.
Geralt and Ciri leave the Isle of Mists together to return to the continent and confront the Wild Hunt, traveling to Kaer Morhen to prepare for a final stand.

After being cured, Avallac'h revealed that he had hidden Ciri on the Isle of Mists, outside time and space, to protect her, keeping her in a magically induced sleep until Geralt arrived and his presence broke the spell, waking her.

At Kaer Morhen, Geralt gathers allies including Yennefer, Triss Merigold, fellow Witchers Eskel and Lambert, and friends Roach and Letho, preparing potions and magical traps ahead of the Wild Hunt's assault.
After reuniting, Geralt and Ciri returned to Kaer Morhen, but Eredin tracked them there with the Wild Hunt.
During the Battle of Kaer Morhen, Eredin's second-in-command Imlerith led the Wild Hunt's assault, and Vesemir sacrificed his life protecting Ciri from him.
Vesemir's death triggered an uncontrolled/grief-driven eruption of Ciri's elder blood power, devastating the attacking Wild Hunt forces and forcing them to retreat.
The defenders of Kaer Morhen only managed to repel Eredin's assault through a stroke of miraculous luck.
Vesemir's body is cremated on a pyre near Kaer Morhen after the battle.
Geralt and his allies hunted down and killed Imlerith to weaken the Wild Hunt.

Following the battle, Geralt's coalition retrieves the Sunstone and allies with the Lodge of Sorceresses to lure Eredin into a trap, leading a coalition of Skellige warriors, Nilfgaardian soldiers, and the Lodge to draw out the Wild Hunt.
Avallac'h convinced the Wild Hunt general Ge'els to stay out of the final conflict.
Geralt and his allies recruited the surviving Lodge of Sorceresses to help summon and trap the Naglfar, Eredin's vessel for traveling between worlds.

The final battle against the Wild Hunt took place off the shores of Skellige; Geralt used a magic elven artifact to summon the Naglfar into a trap in a Skellige bay, while the Lodge of Sorceresses' magic prevented it from fleeing and the imperial fleet blocked its escape to open sea.
As Geralt kills him, Eredin reveals with his final words that Avallac'h has taken Ciri and deceived them both.
Ciri chooses to enter the White Frost herself to use her elder blood power to stop the encroaching entropy of the multiverse.
The Lodge of Sorceresses played an instrumental role in negotiating the Peace of Cintra, ending the Second Nilfgaard War.

King Venzlav of Brugge was a vassal of Cintra but turned to Temeria for protection after Cintra's fall, paying homage to his cousin King Foltest; despite being small and poor, Brugge's people fought valiantly against Nilfgaard, including at the Battle of Brenna.

Aedirn suffered greatly from war with Kaedwen and the Second Nilfgaard War, during which the empire looted and dismantled production centers, and after King Demavend's death Aedirn suffered social disturbances, peasant revolts, renewed conflict with Kaedwen, and a growing separatist movement in the Pontar Valley.
After King Eist's death in the Battle of the Marnadal Dale, the Skellige islanders swore vengeance on the Nilfgaardians and became their implacable enemies.

During the last war against Nilfgaard, Verden betrayed the Northern coalition, paying homage to the empire and attacking Brugge; Prince Kistrin later led a successful rebellion against his treacherous father, returning Verden to the Northern coalition, though it remains viewed with suspicion.

The Nilfgaardian Empire has subjugated Ymlac, Vicovaro, Rowan, Etolia, Gemmera, Maecht, Ebbing, Geso, Mettina, and Nazair over its history, and during the recent Northern Wars added Cintra, the Duchy of Attre, and temporarily Upper Sodden and Verden to its possessions.

During the Northern Wars, the dwarves of Mahakam remained officially neutral but tended to support the Northern Kingdoms, providing arms and forming a volunteer regiment, the Mahakam Volunteer Detachment, which fought valiantly, notably helping halt the elite Nilfgaardian Ard Feainn cavalry division at the Battle of Brenna while encircled.
The Lodge of Sorceresses was later accused of involvement in the Assassinations of Kings, including the deaths of Demavend of Aedirn and Foltest of Temeria, leading to purges and a temporary ban.

Peace accords after the second Nilfgaard war forced Aedirn to cede the Valley of the Flowers (Dol Blathanna), which had been part of Aedirn after being seized from elven hands two centuries prior, back to the elves.
Elves have lost most of their ancient lands to humans over centuries of conflict, only recently regaining an independent realm, Dol Blathanna, after the Northern Wars.
Elven Scoia'tael units fought and died on the side of the empire, buying the establishment of Dol Blathanna with hundreds of elven lives.

The peace treaty creating Dol Blathanna also required Nilfgaard to hand over about three dozen elven officers accused of war crimes to the Northern kings, causing many elves to feel betrayed by Emhyr.
The djinn-wish bond between Geralt and Yennefer is later revisited in The Witcher 3, where they attempt to use another djinn to determine if their love is genuine or magically compelled.
Queen Meve personally organized a guerrilla resistance movement against Nilfgaardian occupation using knights, peasants, and bandits.
Before the final confrontation, Eredin led an assault on Kaer Morhen alongside his second-in-command Imlerith and the riders of the Wild Hunt in an attempt to capture Ciri.

The Mahakam Volunteer Detachment also fought at the battles of Mayena and Maribor, but its contributions are often omitted by historians who credit only allied kingdom armies; its last recognized honor was a victory parade in Novigrad.
Novigrad's new steward of state security reportedly had his predecessor burned at the stake after a public trial.
Geralt of Rivia boarded the ghostly ship of the Wild Hunt after the imperial fleet cut off its escape route to the high seas.

Ciri decided to enter an ancient portal on the Isle of Undvik to confront her destiny and try to stop the White Frost, leaving behind her adoptive father Geralt of Rivia, who had spent a long time searching for her.
Geralt's biological father is rumored in the lore to be a warrior named Corin, though this is never confirmed and Geralt does not dwell on it.
Priest Sigebert preached during the witch hunt period between 1272 and 1276, condemning the theory that humans arrived via the Conjunction of the Spheres as blasphemy invented by the elves.
The circumstances that led to the extinction of the Wozgor and Dauk peoples remain disputed among scholars.
The Nilfgaardian Empire's writings and records from conquered southern territories were largely deposited at the Imperial Academy.
Redania's Royal Corps army fought in both wars against Nilfgaard.
The realm of Jamurlak was reportedly once subject to Redanian rule, formerly ruled by the cruel and lecherous King Abrad, who has since died.
Aedirn developed later than its western neighbors but prospered faster than Kaedwen, due to fertile lands and mineral wealth.
The Nilfgaardian Empire was likely founded by the people of the city of Nilfgaard on the Alba River, which serves as the empire's capital.
Some cruel humans leave sick children infected with diseases like smallpox at the edge of Brokilon Forest hoping to spread epidemics among the dryads.

Brokilon Forest is in a state of perpetual war with the surrounding human lands; neighboring lords covet its valuable trees and the treasures rumored to be hidden in the ruined city and necropolis of Craag An deep within the forest.

For hundreds of years humans have tried to log Brokilon Forest, leading to repeated violent clashes with the dryads; humans execute captured dryads without mercy, while dryads kill any intruders into their forest with arrows, showing no distinction for age or gender.

The kings of Verden and Kerack harbor a legendary hatred of the dryads and their leader due to raids on settlers, though the more moderate king of Brugge has prevented the conflict with Brokilon from escalating into full extermination war.
The hero Zatret Voruta was given to the dwarves as an Unexpected Child because his was the first face his father saw upon returning home.
The hero Supree was an Unexpected Child given to the Mad Dei, whom he later saved from a terrible curse.
The origins and original creators of the witcher training and mutation process are unknown, as those who developed it are long dead.
The Iello Massacre, attributed to the witcher Brehen (later called the Cat of Jello), is one of the infamous episodes tarnishing witchers' reputation.
Sorcerers Cosimo Malaspina and his apprentice Alzur are believed to be the original creators of the witcher mutation process.
Alzur was killed in Maribor by a viy, a giant centipede-like creature he had created himself; the creature then rampaged through half the city before fleeing to Riverdell's forests.
A band of armed assailants once broke into Kaer Morhen and stole some of the witchers' secret knowledge.
Geralt once was approached by a duke to find a girl who rejected his advances and fled leaving a shoe, a task Geralt argued was suited for a huntsman, not a witcher.

According to an anecdote, sorceress Yennefer of Vengerberg once cast a spell using her leg for gesticulation, witnessed by Master Dorregaray in the Kestrel Mountains; a letter from Ban Ard Sorcerer's School describes students getting drunk and staging an obscene contest trying to replicate the feat during Belleteyn celebrations.
Before restrictions were imposed, unrestricted practice of necromancy and demonology caused hundreds of accidental deaths among sorcerers and bystanders.
Conflicts between draconids and humans increased as human settlements expanded into draconid territory.

A golden dragon named Villentretenmerth confronted King Niedamir of Caingorn and his dragon hunters near Woefield, forcing them to retreat; the confrontation was confirmed by multiple eyewitnesses, including two sorcerers and a witcher.
Only two cases of creating a koshchey have ever been recorded, credited to sorcerers Cosimo Malaspina and his apprentice Alzur.
The renegade druid Ferengal created a koshchey to help his band of robbers ambush merchant caravans crossing Klamat Pass, halting trade on that route.

In a folktale, the sorceress Yennefer tried to ensnare a genie in a magical net in the Redanian city of Rinde to use it against local officials who had criticized her lifestyle; the genie escaped her spells and destroyed a dozen buildings before a witcher named Gerhard used a secret exorcism to banish it.
Elven legend speaks of another elf tribe, the Aen Elle ('People of the Alders' or 'Alder Folk'), whose paths diverged from the Aen Seidhe after the Conjunction of the Spheres opened many worlds.
The order of witchers was created specifically to defend humanity against monsters using steel, silver, and magic.
A small number of Wolf School witchers survived the pogrom and continue to use the ruins of Kaer Morhen as a winter shelter and training ground.
The Scoia'tael, elven and nonhuman freedom fighters also called Squirrels, emerged after the First Nilfgaard War, taking advantage of the absence of Northern soldiers who had marched south.
Eternal Fire priests taught that the sacred flame symbolized progress, light dispelling darkness, and hope for the future.
Early Eternal Fire doctrine tolerated other faiths except for blasphemy against the Eternal Fire or attempts to undermine its authority.
Those declared blasphemers or sorcerers who harmed others were burned at the stake by a special temple guard under early Eternal Fire rule.
The kings of the North wanted to prevent Ciri from marrying Emperor Emhyr var Emreis, which would have legitimized his claim to Cintra's throne.

The Lodge of Sorceresses was founded after the Thanedd Coup by powerful female mages who sought revenge on Vilgefortz and wanted to find and educate Ciri, then marry her to a Koviri duke to place a sorceress-aligned ruler on the throne.
Worship of Prophet Lebioda's teachings gradually spread through and displaced the older cult of Kreve across nearly all of Redania, and the movement gained a militant arm.
As the Eternal Fire's influence grew, its hierarch, elected by a college, became the de facto ruler of Novigrad.
The Eternal Fire's temple guard evolved into an unchecked state security force with no secular oversight.
The Church of the Eternal Fire, led by Caleb Menge and the Temple Guard, carried out violent persecution of mages and nonhumans in Novigrad.
Novigrad's underworld was controlled by four crime lords: Sigi Reuven, Sigismund Dijkstra, and the King of Beggars among them.
The Lodge of Sorceresses was a secret organization founded after the fall of the Conclave and Supreme Council, meant to preserve and guide magic's future.
The Order of the Flaming Rose eventually became an extremist group devoted to racial persecution and witch hunts, turning against the humans and nonhumans it once swore to protect.
The Order of the Flaming Rose is a militant arm associated with the spread of Lebiodan faith, known for hostility toward nonhumans and magic.
Novigrad's Eternal Fire cult has recently grown considerably in influence and real power among the city's faithful.
The Scoia'tael are composed mostly of elves, but also include dwarves and halflings, and are known for ambushing settlers, merchants, and soldiers.
Notable Scoia'tael leaders include Faoiltiarna, Iorveth, and Yaevinn.

The Order of the Flaming Rose originated as the secular Order of the White Rose in Temeria, founded on the ideal of defending the innocent and downtrodden, which became focused on land grants and wealth rather than its founding ideals.
After Grand Master Rudolf Valaris died, Jacques de Aldersberg took over and renamed the order the Order of the Flaming Rose, adopting the tenets of the Eternal Fire faith.
After events in Vizima, the Order of the Flaming Rose relocated to Redania and, under King Radovid's protection, became an armed force serving the crown.
The Order of the Flaming Rose received grants of land near Roggeveen in exchange for serving as an armored enforcement arm of the king.
Kaedwen's people harbor lasting disdain for elves due to their war history, and the feeling is mutual.
Despite a reputation as backward due to conflict and forested terrain, the Kaedweni are known as hospitable and friendly, aiding travelers freely.
The Kingdom of Lyria and Rivia has long been Aedirn's staunchest ally, forming a defensive bulwark against Nilfgaard along the Yaruga River.
Each Skellige isle is ruled by a jarl belonging to one of six powerful clans, with an overall king chosen from a major clan during traditional moots.
The Skellige Islands are longtime allies of Cintra through marriage; King Eist Tuirseach of Cintra was brother of Skellige's King Bran and uncle of Jarl Crach an Craite.
The Nilfgaardian Empire lies south of the Yaruga River and has expanded by conquering weaker neighbors over centuries.
Lands conquered by the Nilfgaardian Empire become imperial provinces ruled by appointed governors, while monarchs who willingly submit may retain their titles.
Emhyr var Emreis commands vast professional armies, internal garrison troops, a secret police, and the fanatical personal guard known as the Impera Brigade.
A significant hidden opposition to Emhyr var Emreis's rule exists within the Nilfgaardian Empire.
Dwarves are known for being dependable, honorable, but also grumbling and possessive of their kin and gold, ranking behind only dragons and men in greed.
Dwarves fiercely guard their women, who are considered unattractive by human standards, believing others desire to seduce them.
The dwarven ancestral homeland is the mountainous region of Mahakam, though many dwarves live in human cities working as craftsmen, bankers, merchants, bodyguards, or mercenaries.
Unlike elves, dwarves have pragmatically assimilated many human customs, reducing tension between the races, though prejudice and pogroms against dwarves still occur.
Conservative dwarves and Scoia'tael sympathizers view dwarves who work for humans as traitors.
Gnomes are shorter than dwarves, less strong, but more agile and equally resistant to hardship, known for their long pointy noses.
Gnomes excel at metallurgy, armoring, jewelry-making, and goldsmithing but rarely trade outside their native lands due to fear of human envy and pogroms.
Although Temerian kings are titular lords of Mahakam, the region is largely autonomous, governed by a chosen dwarven elder.
Elves call themselves Aen Seidhe, meaning 'People of the Hills' in their own language.
Elves are tall, slim, with elongated symmetrical faces, large eyes, and slightly pointed ear conchae, and lack canine teeth (despite eating meat).
Elves are extremely long-lived, with lifespans lasting hundreds or even thousands of years, but can only reproduce while young.
Elves and humans can crossbreed to produce fertile half-elf offspring, who often face discrimination in human society.

An anonymous account describes being abducted by the Wild Hunt one autumn night and taken to another world, enduring what felt like endless servitude before escaping back to find years had passed at home.
Brokilon Forest is the last dryad enclave, ruled by Lady Eithne, known as the Silver-Eyed, famed for her wisdom and hostility toward humans.
Dryads, also called 'eerie wives' by humans, once inhabited nearly all forests but now survive only in Brokilon Forest.
Dryads resemble young, slender maidens and the entire race consists exclusively of females, with young dryads born from unions between dryads and elves, or rarely humans.

Due to mostly hostile relations with humans, dryads have taken to kidnapping human girls, giving them the Water of Brokilon to erase their memories so they can be raised as dryads and replenish their numbers.

Some humans reportedly leave sick children (with smallpox, diphtheria, or scarlet fever) at Brokilon's edge hoping to spread disease among dryads, but dryads seem immune and may instead heal such children into new recruits and defenders of the forest.

Dryads deeply revere their forest and would never intentionally harm it, building their homes from living trees they can shape at will, and are exceptionally skilled archers who surpass even elves in mastery of the bow.
Dryads do not recognize human-drawn borders and attack settlers on lands that were formerly part of Brokilon Forest.
Zerrikania is inhabited by warlike clans reportedly led by women, including Free Warriors—tattooed female mercenaries who fight with curved sabers called saberras.
Witchers are described by sorcerers as mutants with superhuman abilities created specifically to kill monsters for money.
Nobles view witchers as tools to solve problems like succession disputes, personal security, and conflicts with other rulers.
Druids consider witchers to be butchers who mindlessly exterminate endangered species for profit.
Common people mostly see witchers as professionals hired to eliminate dangerous creatures, like specialized pest control.
Some people who owe witchers their lives view them as noble defenders of mankind.
Others see witchers as godless, cursed freaks who exploit the poor and desperate for coin.
The clergy generally holds witchers in low esteem, officially because witchers do not worship any gods.
Many witchers historically invoked the Law of Surprise as payment for their services, believing such children would easily pass or be exempt from the witcher trials.
Common folklore claims witchers kidnap children from villages, though this is described as false since abducting children would be impractical for witchers.
Most witcher recruits came from orphans, abandoned children, and unwanted offspring such as bastards or extra sons with no inheritance.
Sorcerers who helped establish witcher training were primarily responsible for seeking out potential recruits.
Only physically and mentally fit boys were selected as witcher candidates, as weaker candidates would not survive training.
Other witcher schools besides Kaer Morhen existed, each with different training programs and processes for the Changes.
The Cat School was notorious for producing witchers who were psychopaths, madmen, and sadists due to flawed mutation processes or selection of aggressive candidates.
Albert Braas wrote about the Witcher Code in his work 'Nordling Tribal Customs', describing it as a strict set of rules governing witcher conduct, most of which remain secret.
The Aen Saevherne are a separate caste of elven sages who reportedly possess knowledge of magic as well as understanding of other worlds, time, and space.

Known members of the Lodge of Sorceresses included Philippa Eilhart, Sile de Tansarville, Sabrina Glevissig, Triss Merigold, Keira Metz, Margarita Laux-Antille, Yennefer of Vengerberg, the elves Francesca Findabair and Ida Emean aep Sivney, and Nilfgaardian sorceresses Assire var Anahid and Fringilla Vigo.
The cult of the Great Sun is the primary religion worshiped in the Nilfgaardian Empire.
Ancient forgotten cults include Coram Agh Tera, Veyopatis, and the mysterious Water Lords.
The cult of Melitele is an ancient religion combining prehuman beliefs about goddesses of harvest, fertility, and love into worship of the Allmother.
Melitele is worshiped in three forms: the maiden, the mother, and the crone.
The Melitele temple school in Ellander teaches reading, writing, arithmetic, philosophy, ethics, history, and healing to children and youths.
The cult of Kreve is popular in Kaedwen, Redania, and Woefield, and its priests are known for political involvement and moralizing.
Druids do not worship a specific deity but proclaim the divinity of nature itself and emphasize maintaining natural balance.
Druid communities are organized into local circles, each led by a chief druid called a hierophant, or a flaminika if the position is held by a woman.
Druids are known for defending endangered species and maintaining good relations with local populations, giving them significant social influence.
The goddess Freya is worshiped chiefly in the Skellige Isles, where she is called modron (mother) and is patron of hearth, love, fertility, and harvest.
Freya is also patron of prophetesses and seers, symbolized by the necklace Brisingamen, the cat, and the falcon.
Skellige Islanders also worship various sea gods and practice an ancestor 'cult of heroes' alongside a local branch of druidism.
The Svalblod cult practiced bloody rites that led to its marginalization and near-total banishment from the Skellige Isles.
