An Eternal Fire priest's sermon condemned women as sinful and demanded they be beaten, dressed modestly, and denied finery to curb supposed promiscuity.
In remote regions, older faiths persist, such as the cult of the Ladies of the Wood in Velen, whose shrines are scattered through forests and villages there.
In some regions, leshens are worshipped as nature deities under the names Kerun or Kernos, with communities sacrificing small game or birds to them.
Lara Dorren aep Shiadhal was an elven sorceress and member of the Aen Saevherne, the Knowing Ones or Sages.
Geralt grew up knowing his mother was alive, which fostered lasting cynicism toward mages and destiny.
Vesemir, the Wolf School's master at arms, became Geralt's primary father figure and mentor.
Geralt's white hair and pale skin earned him the nickname Gwynbleidd, meaning White Wolf.
The additional mutations gave Geralt faster reflexes, superior night vision, and an extremely high resistance to toxins compared to standard witchers.
As a young man, Geralt originally wanted to name himself Geralt Roger Eric du Haute-Bellegarde.
Vesemir mocked Geralt's elaborate chosen name and warned it would get him killed or mocked on the road.
Geralt settled on the surname 'of Rivia' despite having no actual connection to the kingdom of Rivia.
Geralt practiced a Rivian accent to make his invented identity more convincing.
The Blaviken incident made Geralt more reluctant to interfere in human affairs and reinforced his reliance on the Witcher's code as an emotional shield.
Geralt eventually met Vizenna as an adult, and the reunion was cold and distant rather than warm.
The Urcheon of Erlenwald was revealed to be a duke from the south named Duny.
Calanthe never fully trusted her son-in-law Duny/Emhyr var Emreis.
Yennefer had feelings for a fellow mage named Istredd and could not choose between him and Geralt of Rivia, leading her to repeatedly leave and return to Geralt over the years.
Renfri, known as Shrike for her habit of impaling victims, led a gang seeking vengeance against a mage she believed had wronged her.
Gerhart of Aelle was raised by elves and grew up to become the renowned sorcerer known as Hen Gedymdeith.
Sorceress Triss Merigold was believed dead after the Second Battle of Sodden but actually survived her wounds, later becoming known as the Fourteenth of the Hill.
Geralt of Rivia first met Dandelion at a fete in Gulet, in the Kingdom of Aedirn, and the two became close friends who traveled together.
Rather than killing the sylvan, Geralt of Rivia tried to drive it off peacefully, showing he was not indiscriminately violent.
Geralt of Rivia was already a famous folk hero known as the White Wolf before his later deeds affected the fates of kingdoms.
Yennefer initially treated Geralt of Rivia as a useful tool, flirting with him while planning to use him to help capture a genie for her own power.
After reuniting with Ciri, Geralt chose to accept his role as her father, abandoning his belief that he was incapable of love.
Yennefer was so enraged by Geralt of Rivia's abrupt departure that she refused to hear his name mentioned for four years afterward.
Geralt spent six years trying to avoid the responsibility of his claim on Ciri, taking distant contracts and refusing to return to Cintra.
Yennefer of Vengerberg was formerly named Jenny and was admitted to Aretuza's first class after testing confirmed her magical talent.
Yennefer of Vengerberg came from an abusive family; her father abused her physically and psychically, and her mother failed to support her.
Yennefer of Vengerberg suffered from a deformed spinal column and scapula (being a hunchback) and is a quarter elvish, with a half-elf mother.
Yennefer of Vengerberg attempted suicide as a result of childhood trauma and abuse.
Archmistress Tissaia de Vries personally recommended Yennefer of Vengerberg and highly praised her despite her troubled background.
Yennefer of Vengerberg's physical deformities and tendon trauma were corrected using higher magic during her first year at Aretuza.
Ciri was discovered to be a source, a person with dormant magical talents and prophetic abilities.
Yennefer was asked by Geralt of Rivia to guide Ciri's magical instruction, and their initially cold relationship warmed over time.
Calanthe's second husband was Eist Tuirseach, a man from the Skellige Isles.
Yennefer had not participated in the coup at Thanedd, contrary to rumor; she had instead been searching for Ciri and was captured by treacherous former allies.
Geralt of Rivia's search party included Dandelion, Milva, Zoltan Chivay, Emiel Regis Rohellec Terzieff-Godefroy, and Cahir Mawr Dyffryn aep Ceallach.
Cahir Mawr Dyffryn aep Ceallach was a young Nilfgaardian originally sent by Emperor Emhyr var Emreis to find Ciri, but he abandoned his mission to help Geralt's group instead.
Angouleme, a teenage adventuress, joined Geralt of Rivia's group after they crossed the Yaruga into Nilfgaardian-annexed territory.
Avallac'h warned Geralt of Rivia that his search for Ciri was misguided, insisting she did not need protection and that interference with her fate would bring horrendous consequences.
In Toussaint, Geralt of Rivia became close with Fringilla Vigo, a Nilfgaardian sorceress and relative of Anna Henrietta.
After escaping Bonhart, Ciri found shelter with the hermit Vysogota of Corvo, a former Oxenfurt Academy professor exiled for his controversial philosophical writings.
At Tor Zireael, Ciri's inherited Elder Blood awakened, granting her mastery over space and time and making her the Lady of Time and Space.
Philippa Eilhart and Sile de Tansarville were sorceresses who conspired to manipulate the political landscape at Loc Muinne.
Yennefer became a spiritual mother figure to Ciri, deepening her bond with Geralt as they both took on parental roles for her.
The Prophet Lebioda was a simple shepherd who lived about a century and a half before the present, preaching sermons and telling parables about life, gods, and men, and gathering many followers.
Ciri escaped the Aen Elle world by using her growing ability to travel between worlds.
Radovid the Stern emerged as the harshest northern leader, persecuting anyone associated with magic under the guise of protecting the realm.
Prophet Lebioda died being burned and devoured by a dragon he was attempting to exorcise.
Emhyr var Emreis wanted Ciri found in order to secure an heir carrying the Elder Blood to strengthen Nilfgardian dynastic rule.
Geralt accepted Emhyr var Emreis's commission for pragmatic reasons, using imperial resources to find Ciri while intending to protect her autonomy.
The Bloody Baron's storyline, regardless of its ending, ends with him confronting the ruin of his own life.
As a mutant, Geralt becomes a target of the anti-mage, anti-nonhuman bigotry sweeping Novigrad.
In Skellige, Geralt reunites with his old friend Crach an Craite, who had looked after Ciri during her childhood summers.
Avallac'h became Ciri's crucial ally in her flight from the Wild Hunt, putting him in open conflict with Eredin.
Geralt discovers a creature called Uma, found on Skellige's shores after the magical explosion, who carries a curse masking his true identity.
After being found, Ciri describes the Wild Hunt as a constant, physical pressure that pursued her across every world she visited.
Ciri's relationship with Geralt shifts from ward and mentor to equal partners preparing to face the Wild Hunt together.
Geralt considers Vesemir's death the loss of his true father figure and the end of the era of the old Witchers.
After Vesemir's death, Ciri resolves to end Eredin's pursuit for good, displaying a hardened resolve reminiscent of her grandmother Calanthe.
Geralt finds Avallac'h at the center of a magical storm and learns he is not a traitor but a facilitator of Ciri's plan.
Geralt is forced to let Ciri face the White Frost alone, trusting she is strong enough to survive without him.
King Foltest of Temeria, before his assassination, held titles including Duke of Sodden, Sovereign of Pontar and Mahakam, and Senior Protector of Ellander, Brugge, Riverdell, and Angren.
Queen Meve rules Lyria and Rivia and became known as a strong, resourceful leader during the recent war with Nilfgaard, earning comparisons to Calanthe.
King Ethain of Cidaris is considered an enlightened, just, non-interfering ruler; Cidaris supported the Northern coalition's fleet in the last war against Nilfgaard.
Dandelion turned Geralt's grim exploits, including the Blaviken massacre, into romanticized ballads that built Geralt's public legend as the White Wolf.
Dandelion provides Geralt with social connections, gossip, and logistical help that Geralt would otherwise lack living on the road.
As a Witcher, Geralt is sterile due to his mutations, making the idea of having a child deeply ironic to him.
Letho of Gulet is a member of the largely extinct School of the Viper, known for combining brute strength with a sharp tactical mind.
Novigrad's hierarch Cyrus Engelkind Hemmelfart is an old, slothful man known for racism but not particularly active in persecuting nonhumans.
Emperor Emhyr var Emreis rules Nilfgaard as an absolute sovereign, though a ceremonial senate exists.
Emhyr var Emreis's full Elder Speech title, Deithwen Addan yn Carn aep Morvudd, means 'White Flame Dancing on the Barrows/Graves of His Enemies.'
Mahakam's dwarven elder, Brouver Hoog, is known for his strict adherence to tradition and controversial decrees, and spoke against dwarves joining Scoia'tael units.
Dol Blathanna (Valley of the Flowers) is ruled by the elven sorceress Enid an Gleanna, known as Francesca Findabair among humans and considered the most beautiful woman in the world.
Francesca Findabair's chief advisor is Filavandrel aen Fidhail of the Silver Towers, leader of the Free Elves of the Blue Mountains, also known as Filavandrel of the World's End.
The Aen Elle were supposedly led by Auberon Muircetach, known as the King of the Alders, who ruled from the city of Tir nd Lia.
Geralt of Rivia was believed to be an Unexpected Child claimed through the Law of Surprise.
Geralt of Rivia survived the Trial of the Grasses and the Changes, losing hair pigment as a result, but the rest of his test group did not survive.
The sorcerer Alzur was famous for his powerful voice and superior diction, which let him cast even highly complex spells with ease.
Emhyr var Emreis, Emperor of Nilfgaard, expected obedience and results from sorcerers serving the Empire, threatening punishment for disobedience or failure.
Yennefer of Vengerberg's experiences at the Temple of Freya on Hindarsfjall somewhat shook her skepticism about the existence of gods.
Vesemir reportedly said holy symbols are useless against vampires, at most insulting their religious feelings if they have any.
Vilgefortz of Roggeveen was a renowned hero of the Battle of Sodden Hill, a member of the Chapter of Mages, and a decorated veteran of the First Nilfgaard War before his treason was revealed.
Through her mother Pavetta, grandmother Calanthe, and ancestor Riannon, Ciri is a direct descendant of the elven Sage Lara Dorren aep Shiadhal.
Avallac'h claimed his goal in using the Gate of the Worlds was to save the Aen Seidhe elves and humans from the White Frost.
Eredin's true motives for controlling the Gate of the Worlds were suspected to be conquest of other worlds rather than salvation.
Jacques de Aldersberg was revealed to be a source, a person born with innate magical power.
Jacques de Aldersberg's ultimate goal was to breed a new race of supermen able to survive the White Frost prophesied by Ithlinne.
Avallac'h is an Aen Saevherne, a powerful elven mage-sage.
At the start of the Third Witcher game, Geralt arrives in White Orchard, a village devastated by the Third Northern War and Nilfgardian occupation.

After Velen, Geralt's search for Ciri continued in Novigrad, a city that had become gripped by religious paranoia and persecution under the Eternal Fire, though it was once known as a free city and center of trade and intellectual life.
Dandelion gave Geralt a home base in the city of Novigrad.
East of Tir Tochair lies the Korath Desert, also called the Frying Pan by those living on its edge.
Kovir and Poviss are rich lands on the Gulf of Praxeda, with vassal duchies of Talgar, Velhad, and Narok.

Redania is located between the Buina and Pontar Rivers, holds sovereignty over the Arc Coast, the Nimnar Valley, and Gelibol, and its capital is Tretogor, though its cultural pride is Oxenfurt and its famous university.

Kaedwen's capital is Ard Carraigh, but its most famous city is Ban Ard, home to a sorcerers' school considered the male equivalent of Aretuza, though less prestigious and better known for its heavy cavalry banner than academic achievement.

Temeria's northern border is the Pontar River, bordering Cidaris to the west and Kaedwen, Aedirn, and Lyria to the east via the Mahakam Massif; the Temerian kings hold court at Vizima, located on a lake shore, and other important cities include Maribor, fortified Mayena, and the port city of Gors Velen, near the Aretuza sorceresses' school.
Aedirn's cities Gulet and Eysenlaan are metallurgy centers, while Aldersberg and the capital Vengerberg house textile workshops, dyeworks, and distilleries.

Novigrad is the greatest port on the Great Sea, home to more than a dozen major merchant companies, four water mills, a mint, eight banks, nineteen pawnshops, nearly forty inns, a dozen brothels, and nearly two dozen temples mostly dedicated to the Eternal Fire.
Lyria contains the Dol Angra region, one of only two locations suitable for mass crossings of the Yaruga River, defended by the fortresses of Spalla and Scalla.

Cidaris owes its wealth to marine trade, fishing, pearl hunting, amber mining, and famous vineyards; its Sea Bazaar hosts goods from around the world, and its shipyards launch several hundred ships per year.
Verden, Brugge, and Kerack lie in the shadow of Brokilon Forest, home to hostile dryads.
Kerack is known for corruption, its only notable feature being the inn Natura Rerum.
Verden was once a vassal of Cintra, now occupied by the Nilfgaardian Empire, and holds a strategic position at the mouth of the Yaruga with the fortresses of Nastrog, Rozrog, and Bodrog.
Mahakam lies between Temeria to the west and Aedirn/Lyria to the east, and is famous for producing the best steel and finest weapons in the world.

Prospective witchers were trained at Kaer Morhen, also known as the Witchers' Seat, home of the Wolf School; its name derives from the Elder Speech phrase 'caer a'muirehen,' meaning 'old sea keep,' suggesting it was originally an elven structure, and it is believed to be located in the inaccessible mountains of northeastern Kaedwen along the upper reaches of the Gwenllech river.
Witchers spend winters at Kaer Morhen resting, restocking potions, repairing equipment, and reuniting with other witchers.

Places of Power are locations with extremely high circulation of magical energy, often found at tectonic plate boundaries, water vein intersections, volcanic zones, swamps, and windswept cliffs; sorcerers often build towers at such sites, which were historically places of worship with megaliths and temples.

Aretuza, located in the palace on the island of Thanedd off Temeria's shores, is the school where young female adepts are trained as sorceresses; only sorceresses and trainees are allowed on Thanedd itself, with visitors and petitioners restricted to the palace of Loxia guarding the bridge to Gors Velen.
A major center of the cult of Melitele is a temple-cloister complex near Ellander in Temeria, administered by the priestess Nenneke.
The Sedna Abyss is a feared location near Skellige where ships have vanished without a trace.

Kidnapped human girls are said to be given the Water of Brokilon, which erases their former memories, after which the dryads raise them as their own; Ciri survived exposure to this memory-depleting water while in the dryads' forest.
Though the original cult around Prophet Lebioda largely died out after his death, his teachings were preserved in a text called the Good Book, a collection of parables and anecdotes.
Vysogota of Corvo told Ciri about the Tower of the Swallow, Tor Zireael, which housed a teleport magically linked to Tor Lara on Thanedd.

The spell known as Merigold's Ravaging Hailstorm was informally named after Triss Merigold, who created it by accident in 1268 while trying to cast Alzur's Thunder during the pogrom in Rivia, ending the massacre and riots there but never being officially recognized or reproduced.
An investigating commission concluded Triss Merigold's mouth injuries during the Rivia riots caused her to unintentionally distort Alzur's original spell formula, creating the Ravaging Hailstorm.

An alternate theory holds that the Ravaging Hailstorm resulted from Triss Merigold casting in cooperation with Yennefer of Vengerberg, but this was rejected due to lack of evidence Yennefer was in Rivia.
Geralt and Yennefer use the Mask of Uroboros to witness magical echoes of the past on Ard Skellig.
Alzur created spells such as Alzur's Shield and Alzur's Thunder that are still used by sorcerers today.
A book titled Monstrum; or, A Portrayal of Witchers was published, spreading exaggerated and false accusations against witchers, likely authored by a member of the clergy.

Witcher medallions are magically imbued silver items that serve as both practical tools and symbols of guild membership, reacting to nearby sorcerous auras, spellcasting, illusions, and magical creatures, and warning of sudden danger.
Original gwyhyr swords are extremely rare and command very high prices.
The witcher medallion can behave abnormally near very strong magical auras, such as Places of Power or during solstices, or in cities full of magical amulets and alarms.

Witcher potions are brewed from ingredients such as monster organs and rare herbs, and are typically lethal or harmful to ordinary humans; witchers are inured to them from childhood training but still suffer ill effects and must take precise doses.
Witcher potions increase toxin resistance, boost regeneration, enhance concentration for casting Signs, speed reflexes, and increase pain tolerance.
Overdosing on witcher potions can be fatal, a known occupational hazard for witchers.
Dimeritium is a rare bluish metal that blocks magic by limiting the flow of the Power around it.
Dimeritium alloyed with iron is used to make shackles that prevent spellcasters from using magic; its touch causes nausea and vertigo.
The most powerful mages can build immunity to dimeritium over time or temporarily neutralize its anti-magic aura.
Alzur's Thunder is a spell capable of killing half a dozen men at once, but it is rarely used because its incantation is extremely complex.
The magic megascope is an artifact allowing mages to communicate at great distance or spy on people and places, replacing crystal balls as the primary communication tool.
The alraunum decoction is known for granting longevity.
Tor Lara, also called Benavent's Portal, is an ancient, unpredictable magical teleport located at the top of Gull Tower on the Isle of Thanedd, with unknown destination and operating principles.

Every witcher, including Geralt, carries two custom-made swords sized to the wielder: a steel sword for humans and mundane creatures, and a silver sword for monsters born of the Conjunction of the Spheres.

Witcher silver swords are considered magical, forged from inherently magical silver, making them lethal to creatures born of evil or magical powers, including relics of the Conjunction of the Spheres and beings created by curses or summoning.
Witcher steel swords are commonly called 'star iron' swords because they are believed to be forged from siderite, an iron meteorite.
Not all witcher steel swords are made from siderite; some are made from magnetite ore or hematite ore.
Dwarven sihils incorporate ancient gnomish grinding and sharpening techniques but are considered inferior to ancient gnomish gwyhyr swords.
Gwyhyrs were ancient gnomish swords made of hollowed dark steel, flame-bladed and extremely sharp, capable of cutting a floating batiste shawl in half.
Magnetite steel is extremely hard and difficult to sharpen, so its core is usually sheathed in softer steel for honing.
The silver sword is not made entirely of silver; its core and edges are steel coated in silver, since silver alone is too soft to sharpen properly.
The silver sword is fragile and should not be used to parry blows.
A wooden stake through the heart can harm a vampire due to their resilience, but a silver sword is the preferred weapon for witchers.
During the Thanedd Coup, Vilgefortz of Roggeveen revealed his true traitorous allegiance and brutally defeated Geralt of Rivia in single combat using a magical steel club.
The Battle of Kaer Morhen is fought against the Wild Hunt, who arrive amid a magical frost storm with spectral ships.
The final battle against the Wild Hunt takes place on the shores of Undvik in the Skellige Isles.

Geralt duels Eredin Bréacc Glas, king and commander of the Wild Hunt, aboard the dying ship Naglfar, ultimately killing him and breaking the Wild Hunt's power for good; Eredin fights with cold precision and world-jumping abilities, while Geralt fights with desperation using every sign and oil available to him in a long, difficult duel.
The Crones of Crookback Bog, named Brewess, Weavess, and Whispess, are ancient malevolent entities who once hosted Ciri and later tried to consume her for her blood's power.
The Crones of Crookback Bog demanded blood and obedience from local peasants in exchange for protection.
Ghouls form the main body of necrophages and include larger dangerous breeds like alghouls, graveirs, and cemetaurs.
Ghouls have a stooped posture, hypertrophied forelimbs, clawed hands adapted for digging, and strong jaws for cracking bones to eat marrow.
Rotfiends and greater rotfiends were once thought to be deformed ghouls but were later classified as a separate necrophage species.
Rotfiends stand upright with human-like limb proportions but have underdeveloped jaws and prefer eating corpses several months old.
Rotfiends rely mainly on smell to find victims since their heads are bloated and nearly eyeless.
Drowners live in both natural and artificial bodies of water, from rivers and lakes to sewers.
Popular belief holds that drowners are the risen corpses of drowned men, but they are actually post-Conjunction creatures.
Drowners and the drowned dead are strong swimmers who sense water vibrations and see well in low light.
Drowners prefer ambush attacks, dragging victims underwater and strangling them with clawed hands.
Water hags live in wetlands, swamps, and bogs, building hovels of wood, mud, and reed or lairing in dug-out hollows.
Water hags have withered, slime-covered bodies, seaweed-like hair, crooked teeth, and werewolf-sized claws, and they throw balls of mud in combat.
Grave hags resemble tall, wizened old women with oversized heads, bulging eyes, and long clawed arms.
Grave hags dig up graves for skulls and bones to decorate their lairs or wear as amulets, leading to the mistaken belief they are female ghouls.
Unlike typical necrophages, grave hags actively hunt or lure victims, skin them, then cook and eat them like human dishes.
Fleders and ekimmaras are not native to the Northern Kingdoms but have expanded their range north across the Yaruga over the past couple decades.
Lesser vampires are more primitive and instinct-driven than higher vampires, vulnerable to sunlight, and hunt only at night.
Fleders will drink blood from and eat the flesh of sick victims and scavenge fresh corpses, behavior other vampire species avoid.
Fleders hibernate in crypts and abandoned buildings during winter, emerging to hunt on the first warm spring nights.
Wraiths are vengeful ghosts of people who died violently or suddenly due to injustice, betrayal, or murder.
Murderers, oath breakers, and kinslayers can also become wraiths after death, not only their victims.
Ghosts of madmen or cruel people often become violent wraiths immediately, while others take time to transform.
Wraiths formed from murder victims may initially seek help from the living for revenge or restitution before fading away, unless powerful emotions bind them to the world.
One theory holds that a wraith's grotesque form reflects growing madness distorting both its inner and outer self over decades or centuries.
Folk belief holds that noonwraiths and nightwraiths are the ghosts of women who died violently before or after their weddings.
Noonwraiths appear on bright, warm days as tanned girls or hags in white robes, sometimes wearing wedding wreaths, preying on field workers and children.
Nightwraiths are active at night, especially during a full moon, ambushing late travelers or sneaking into homes to attack sleepers.
Both noonwraiths and nightwraiths drain life from victims while swirling around them in a mockery of a wedding dance.
Griffins resemble a cross between a large cat and a predatory bird, nesting on inaccessible mountain peaks and preying on large hoofed mammals.
Griffins are highly territorial and will attack travelers, merchant caravans, and shepherds who encroach on their territory.
The archgriffin is a rare, extremely aggressive griffin subspecies capable of spitting acid balls that cause severe burns.
Harpies have the bodies of old women combined with bird wings, talons, and beaks, and they build colonies on inaccessible cliffs.
Harpies are omnivorous, generally attack smaller prey by diving from above, but can gang up on larger prey including armed humans.
The cockatrice, also called the scoffin, is a rare ornithosaur combining traits of birds and reptiles, supposedly hatched from an egg laid by a rooster and incubated by snakes.
Contrary to superstition, a cockatrice's gaze cannot kill or petrify; its real threats are its beak and sharp tail used in ambush or combat.
Werewolves are terianthropes, humans able to transform into wolf or half-wolf hybrid form, usually during a full moon.
Some lycanthropes retain control and avoid people while transformed, while most either embrace bloodlust or black out during transformation.
Botchlings are created when an unwanted child dies and is not properly buried; they are about one and a half feet tall.
A botchling hides under beds and drains vitality from pregnant women, causing fever and weakness before attacking directly and killing mother and unborn child.
When threatened, a botchling can transform into a deformed crawling humanoid to attack with bites and claws.
A striga is created when a cursed pregnant woman's child, or a cursed person who died and was buried, rises years later as a monster instead of surviving as human.
A striga is small, thickset, and hunched, but supernaturally fast, agile, and strong, making it dangerous even to experienced fighters.
Strigas usually hunt at night and become more aggressive during a full moon, though some attack during daytime.
Strigas feed on the flesh and blood of humans and animals, preferring internal organs like the liver and heart.
Lesser draconids include slyzards, forktails, and wyverns, which share scaly skin, bony plate armor, bat wings, and reptilian features with true dragons.
Lesser draconids have atrophied forelegs, with wyverns and forktails having none at all, but possess long flexible necks for fast striking attacks.
True dragons are larger than lesser draconids, with two pairs of well-developed legs, huge wings and tails, and greater intelligence and cunning.
The arachas is an insectoid predator originally native to the far South that has spread north over a few decades, adapting to colder climates by hibernating in mud or forest beds.
The arachas has a chitinous carapace covering its trunk and limbs, with a vulnerable abdomen it protects using shells or hollow logs as makeshift armor.
The arachas ambushes prey by launching a long tendril from its maw to pull victims toward itself, and some subspecies use mimicry to surprise victims.
Endregas are insectoids that live in colonies divided into castes, including workers who tend cocoons and larvae, and warriors who defend the nest and hunt.
Endregas are highly territorial and will attack any creature that approaches their nests, and growing colonies can threaten nearby human settlements.
The koshchey is an artificially created monster resulting from magical experiments, resembling a giant chitinous arachnid several meters long with powerful spiked pincers.
A koshchey is created by magically stimulating the growth of a regular uropygid until it reaches enormous size, retaining the strength-to-size ratio of a normal arachnid.
Golems are magical constructs made by sorcerers from stone, clay, or wood to perform designated tasks such as carrying loads or fighting.
A golem is typically animated by a magical stone called a golem heart placed in its chest.
Golems have no will of their own and can only follow their creator's simple instructions, but they compensate with supernatural resilience and strength.
Golems used as guardians may continue their duties even after their creator's death.
Nekkers are small, misshapen creatures that live in colonies in dark woods, damp gullies, and shadowy dales, connected by underground tunnels.
Nekkers communicate through screeches, grunts, and moans that some scholars theorize may be a primitive language.
Nekkers hunt in packs, ambushing prey from underground tunnels and mobbing cornered victims, though they often hesitate before attacking due to low individual courage.
Larger, more aggressive nekkers called nekker warriors are identifiable by colorful clay smeared on their snouts and often lead groups of smaller nekkers.
Trolls are huge, strong, but not very intelligent creatures that are surprisingly skilled at carpentry and stonemasonry, building resilient structures like bridges.
Trolls often live near bridges and demand tolls of provisions, livestock, or horses from travelers, sometimes eating travelers who have nothing to offer.
Some intelligent trolls make deals with nearby villages, maintaining bridges and even protecting peasants from bandits or predators in exchange for goods.
Wilder mountain trolls sometimes still attack travelers and harass villages, especially in early spring when winter food stores run low.

The leshen, also called the Forest One or Wood One, is a shapeshifter inhabiting ancient forests, able to take forms from a bark-skinned old man to a horned deer-skulled beast or various forest animals.
A leshen can command the forest and its creatures to aid it in battle, making it highly dangerous and earning it the title of lord of the forest.
Leshens are highly territorial, often treating armed intruders such as bandits or hunters as threats to be driven off or eliminated.
Fiends and chorts are large beasts with bulging fur-covered torsos, goat-like hind legs, and antlers (fiends) or curved ram-like horns (chorts).
Fiends rarely leave their deep forest lairs, but when they do, their size and aggression cause catastrophic damage to nearby regions.
Ciri's victory over the White Frost destroys the Wild Hunt and saves the continent from being frozen; some accounts frame this as inferred from the world enjoying a glorious summer afterward.
Geralt of Rivia's story concludes with one of three possible fates for Ciri, depending on the player's choices.
In the Witcher ending, Ciri fakes her death to escape her destiny and Geralt gives her a custom silver sword at an inn in White Orchard, welcoming her as a fellow Witcher.
In the Empress ending, Ciri decides to travel to Nilfgaard and take the throne as the Emperor's successor to bring peace to the continent, parting from Geralt at White Orchard.
In the death ending, Ciri fails to return from the White Frost if Geralt did not provide her enough emotional support and autonomy, leaving Geralt broken.
In the death ending, Geralt returns to Velen to hunt the last remaining crone and recover Ciri's lost medallion, ultimately dying in the swamp.
After the main story, Geralt may retire to the vineyard of Corvo Bianco in Toussaint, finding peace with either Yennefer or Triss.
Geralt of Rivia emerged victorious from his duel with Eredin, breaking the power of the Wild Hunt permanently.

The Trial of the Grasses is a brutal alchemical process involving mutagenic potions administered over several days, meant to mutate child recruits into witchers; it causes severe fevers, vomiting, and hemorrhages, killing most who undergo it.
Only about three out of every ten children who undergo the Trial of the Grasses at Kaer Morhen survive to become witchers.
Geralt of Rivia invoked the Law of Surprise, demanding 'that which Duny already had, though he did not know it.'
Geralt's amnesia after the Wild Hunt ordeal serves as the foundational mystery driving the events of the first Witcher game.
Despite losing his memories, Geralt retained his combat skills and ability to cast Witcher Signs.
The player can choose whether to kill or spare Letho of Gulet after learning of his role in the regicides.
Geralt performed a ritual on the Botchling, the cursed spirit of the Bloody Baron's unborn child, choosing to either destroy it or transform it into a guardian spirit called a Lubokin.
The mutations that created witchers also dampen emotional responses to help them face monsters without fear.
Witcher trainees were encouraged to adopt surnames so they would appear trustworthy to clients rather than seeming like nameless drifters.
The Witcher's Code theoretically requires witchers to remain neutral in human wars, politics, and religious conflicts.
There is no single official written code for witchers; the code is largely an informal professional convention.
Geralt uses five basic combat Signs: Aard for telekinetic force, Igni for flame, Yrden for magical traps, Quen for a protective shield, and Axii for mind manipulation.
Witcher signs are a weaker form of magic compared to full sorceress spellcasting, but are effective combat tools.
Geralt relies on a heightened sensory ability called Witcher's sense to track scents and hear hidden monsters.
Witchers use alchemical oils on blades and decoctions in their blood to temporarily boost combat abilities, though these are highly toxic even to mutated witcher biology.
Under the effects of strong alchemical potions, a witcher's skin pales further, veins darken, and eyes turn black.
Early stages of witcher training involved herbal infusions and a diet of cave fungi to regulate metabolism and boost growth rate before the Trial of the Grasses.
Survivors of the initial Trial of the Grasses underwent a further stage called the Changes, involving more infusions and infections causing additional suffering.
Special experimental trials with new elixirs and mutagens were sometimes performed on witcher trainees, causing extreme suffering to those chosen.
Witcher mutations slow the aging process considerably, allowing witchers to live far longer than ordinary humans, though the exact maximum lifespan is unknown due to violent deaths in the profession.
Witchers have full immunity to disease as a result of their mutations.
Witchers have increased but not complete resistance to venoms and toxins, and also a higher tolerance for alcohol.
Witchers can adjust their pupils to see in darkness or avoid being blinded by sudden light.
Witchers have a slower pulse that can be regulated under stress, heightened reflexes, acute hearing, and increased pain resistance.
Witchers are rendered sterile by their mutations, though it is unclear if this is an intentional measure or a side effect.
Witchers are trained and genetically adjusted to better control their emotions, though they are not truly soulless as popular belief suggests.
Witchers can still feel fear but are trained to control it rather than being fearless.
Witchers can feel compassion for victims of curses, but must be able to act decisively against a monster when necessary despite that empathy.

Witcher training includes physical regimens performed on an obstacle course at Kaer Morhen known as the Path, nicknamed the Gauntlet by trainees; it is dangerous and ever-changing, having injured or killed many young trainees over the years.
The witcher combat style emphasizes speed, mobility, and brutal effectiveness, originally compiled from the techniques of mercenaries and cutthroats before being refined over generations.
Witcher swordsmanship was influenced by elven fencing concepts that favored light armor and relied on dodges and feints rather than heavy armor.
Witchers avoid heavy armor like chainmail or breastplates because such gear hinders the mobility needed to fight multiple monsters or creatures with unconventional attacks like tentacles or pincers.
Witcher training emphasizes fighting in adverse conditions, such as blindfolded, on unstable surfaces, or in water, to prepare for realistic monster encounters.
Witchers study extensive monster lore, including ancient texts, tomes, records, and oral and written tales and legends, to learn enemy habitats, habits, diets, and weaknesses before engaging them.
Before accepting a contract, a witcher must investigate by talking to witnesses, identifying victims, examining the attack scene, and following trails.
Witcher Signs are simple compared to true sorcery but require only concentration and a small gesture, useful since one of a witcher's hands is often occupied by a sword.
Learning Signs requires only minimal magical talent, unlike full sorcery.
In spring, witchers travel the world seeking work by asking innkeepers, reeves, and village aldermen, or checking notices posted at crossroads.
A witcher may refuse any contract that is beneath his dignity, offers inadequate pay, or seems unwinnable.
Payment for witcher contracts is negotiated beforehand and typically paid as a lump sum after job completion, sometimes with an advance for long jobs.
Witchers accept coin from villagers but prefer bank transfers or checks from wealthy clients, redeemable at dwarven banks.

Sorcerers channel the Power flowing through nature and bound within the four elements, since casting spells using only personal vitality is dangerous and can cause weakness, unconsciousness, or death.
Novice sorcerers experience 'contraction,' an uncontrolled acquisition of magical energy that usually causes harmless shocks but can lead to severe harm if precautions are ignored.
Reckless channeling of the Power can cause hemorrhage, nerve shock, blindness, coma, permanent sensory delusions, madness, or catatonia.
Water is considered the safest and most moderate element for inexperienced sorcerers to learn channeling, especially at water vein intersections.
The sea is a powerful but dangerous source of magical energy due to its dynamism, best used only by experienced sorcerers.
Earth is a widely accessible element but inefficient for channeling due to its static nature, though mastery grants exceptional power.
Air is easier to draw upon than earth but requires great skill due to its capricious, dynamic nature.
Fire provides energy quickly but is the most dangerous and unpredictable element, easiest to 'contract' upon, and especially risky for sources.
Powerful sorcerers can sometimes bind a genius to gain near-omnipotent magical power, drawing energy directly from it instead of traditional channeling.
Casting a spell typically requires uttering a magical formula and performing gestures, but the essential requirements are deep concentration and expenditure of accumulated energy.
A sorcerer can only use as much Power as they have channeled; attempting to use more causes severe harm to their own body.
Sorcerers must use only the precise amount of Power needed for a spell's effect, as wasting excess energy on simple tasks is a common novice mistake.
Clear, firm incantation and concise gestures are important for successful spellcasting; stammering can cause spell failure or even fatal magical backlash.
Wands and magical staves are common substitutes for hand gestures in spellcasting.
Spells are formally classified into categories including psychokinetic spells, illusions, divination, transformations, and creation magic, the last considered the pinnacle of sorcery.
Necromancy and demonology (also called goetia) are forbidden fields of magic under the edicts of the Conclave.
The ban on necromancy applies only to practical use, not to theoretical or academic study of the subject.
The Conclave can grant special dispensation allowing study of necromancy in some cases with sufficiently positive applications.
Some sorcerers retain basic theoretical knowledge and rudimentary necromantic skills, such as acquiring simple information from the recently deceased.
Goetia (demonology) involves summoning creatures from other dimensions, often to bargain for information or services.
Summoning a demon does not require great skill, only access to the correct magical formulae, making goetia tempting for novice sorcerers.
Because summoned beings are extremely dangerous, unskilled goetists attempting summoning usually die as a result.
Sorcerers who summon otherworldly creatures without authorization face prohibitions and punishments under Conclave law.
A dwimveandra is a sorceress who, after finishing education at Aretuza, travels and trains under various sorcerers instead of taking a single mistress.
After several years as a traveling dwimveandra, a sorceress may take an exam to earn the title of Mistress of Magic.

A wraith ritual to prevent a restless dead from rising involves drinking moonshine, wrapping a thornapple rod around the corpse's neck, driving nails through its heart, and filling its mouth with poppy seeds before reburial.
Curses require a human caster with sufficiently concentrated will and strong emotion, similar in mechanism to prayer, though the final effect is delayed and rarely matches the literal words spoken.
Witchers are sometimes hired to lift curses on such creatures rather than simply kill them, depending on the circumstances.
Giving a botchling a proper burial lifts its curse and turns it into a protective household spirit called a lubberkin.
The curse can be lifted from a striga by waiting at its burial site through the night until the third crowing of a rooster catches it outside its coffin, returning it to human form.
Esterhazy of Fano is a master swordsmith who wrote about witcher and dwarven weapon-making in 'Tales of Weapons'.
Roderick de Novembre wrote 'The History of the World,' which recounts the legend of Jan Bekker calming the seas.
This information on geniuses comes from Giambattista's 'Elemental Empires.'
The narrator, Dandelion, leaves several questions unanswered at the end of his tale, including the fates of Ciri, Geralt of Rivia, Yennefer, and Zoltan Chivay.
Vilgefortz of Roggeveen secretly planned to betray Emhyr var Emreis and use Ciri to gain power over time and space.
Fringilla Vigo seduced Geralt of Rivia to spy on him, acting on behalf of the secret Lodge of Sorceresses rather than Emperor Emhyr var Emreis.

A note found near a headless corpse in Novigrad's sewers suggests that the criminal organization Salamandra, led by the renegade sorcerer Azar Javed, attempted to seize hidden 'witcher secrets' from Kaer Morhen.
Lifting Uma's curse reveals that the creature is actually the elven sage Avallac'h.

Ciri's true father is Emhyr var Emreis, the emperor of Nilfgaard, a fact kept secret from nearly everyone including Geralt of Rivia for a long time; Emhyr was in fact Duny, the Urcheon of Erlenwald whose curse Geralt lifted, later revealed to be heir to the Nilfgaardian throne.
The mage who had been secretly collaborating with Emhyr var Emreis for years, and who told him of Ithlinne's prophecy, was later revealed to be Vilgefortz of Roggeveen.
Elves are believed to have arrived from another world through magical gates or portals, similar to how humans later arrived.
Ciri did not board the ship during the faked shipwreck, likely because Pavetta, herself a powerful source, saw through Emhyr's plan and protected her daughter.
White Orchard exposes Geralt to the cold, bureaucratic style of Nilfgardian occupation compared to the chaotic cruelty of northern lords.
Geralt's time in Velen prepares him emotionally for his eventual reunion with Ciri.
Geralt often quotes the line 'If I'm to choose between one evil and another, I'd rather not choose at all,' though he repeatedly fails to remain neutral.
Geralt's survival of the experimental mutations at Kaer Morhen is linked to his destined role as Ciri's protector.

The Bloody Baron's questline in Velen serves as a mirror for Geralt's own fears about fatherhood and failing to protect Ciri, and functions as a warning about how personal failings can destroy a father-daughter bond.

The people of Skellige, especially Crach an Craite, consider Ciri family and offer help without political motive, unlike the Emperor of Nilfgaard, making it the only place where Ciri is seen as a person rather than a prophecy.
Human history according to the narrator is defined largely by repeated cycles of war and conquest.
Some scholars believe Wozgor and Dauk beliefs survive today in the religion of Melitele and lesser cults such as Coram Agh Tera and Veyopatis.
Legends claim the sands of the Korath Desert cover the necropolises and catacombs of a long-forgotten, extinct civilization.
Human dominion over the known world was achieved over a few centuries by forcing other races to acknowledge human supremacy or retreat/perish.
An apocryphal version of Ithlinne's prophecy may refer to the people of Haakland as a storm from the East that will burn, slaughter, and feast on the ruins of its enemies.
According to a rejected manuscript, siderite meteorites absorb elemental energy while falling through the Spheres of Fire, Air, Earth, and Water, giving the resulting steel magical properties.

Witcher steel swords earned the derogatory nickname 'swords for men' because they are primarily used against humans who threaten witchers out of hatred, greed, or resentment; some witchers historically also called them 'swords for fools' because so many foolish people tried to kill witchers and were killed instead.
Witchers maintain neutrality, refusing to take sides in the world's political or religious conflicts, which allows them to work regardless of circumstances.
An anonymous quote attributed to Vesemir states that while witchers claim neutrality, sometimes a witcher must act against grave injustice, then walk away expecting no thanks.

There is no single official 'Witcher Code'; the term is used by Geralt to describe his personal principles, and every witcher effectively has his own code, useful for politely declining undesirable jobs since people respect those seen as following principles.

Witchers exist specifically to kill monsters that threaten human life, not sapient beings, harmless creatures, or exotic species; they are not knights-errant fighting for glory but work strictly for money, and do not act as law enforcement pursuing bandits or take sides in wars among rulers.

Magic is often called 'the Art' because it requires rare creative talent and artistry, is also described as chaos incarnate—a dangerous and destructive primal force that emerged from the Conjunction of the Spheres—and is viewed as a science, a discipline of study and progress that began with the Conjunction.

According to Mistress Agnes of Glanville's writing, only cats and dragons among earthly creatures can channel the Power, and both are drawn to magical intersections that other animals avoid; some scholars theorize dragons use accumulated Power to enable flight since their size and mass should make natural flight physically impossible, while cats use it to perceive invisible beings and other-dimensional creatures.
Some prominent sorcerers criticize the field of magic as having reached a deadlock, citing lack of ethics, veneration of outdated theories, and excessive political interest among practitioners.
Tissaia de Vries theorized that prayer allows priests to enter a trance or self-hypnosis, letting them subconsciously channel the Power similar to how sorcerers cast spells.

New religious movements on the Continent increasingly claim exclusive possession of truth, branding other faiths as sinful apostasy, and focus more on enforcing intolerant commandments than on offering spiritual support to their followers.
Most dragon hunts are motivated by greed for treasure rather than genuine desire to eliminate a threat or gain fame.
According to Hallbjorn's account, storms over Skellige were long believed to occur whenever the royal blood of Cintra was spilled, including after the deaths of Adalja and Calanthe.

Boethius of Lyria argued the Rivia Pogrom was a planned provocation, with weapons smuggled in and distributed to human rioters directed at nonhuman districts, while Master Casper Dubhen argued it resulted from common human traits like ignorance and xenophobia rather than conspiracy.
Dandelion compares a good tale to a feast that should end while the audience is neither thirsty nor drunk, paraphrasing a philosopher.

events.summary: Long before humans, ancient races such as gnomes, dwarves, vrans, werebbubbs and relict creatures already inhabited the world, with gnomes and dwarves settling peacefully in Mahakam and Tir Tochair millennia ago.

The Conjunction of the Spheres, roughly 1500 years before the present, brought magic, humans, monsters, vampires and necrophages into the world, and elves arrived from 'white ships' beginning a long colonization.
Elven colonization caused sporadic conflict with dwarves, vrans and werebbubbs, though relations never escalated to total war.

Elven sage Lara Dorren, destined by prophecy to bear a child able to control the Gates of Time, instead bound herself to human mage Cregennan of Lod; both died soon after, but their bloodline survived to become the ancestry of Cirilla.

Human exiles began the true settlement of the Northern Kingdoms around five hundred years before the present in the Landing of the Exiles, founding realms like Redania and Temeria, often atop destroyed elven cities such as Xin'trea (Cintra).

Over subsequent centuries, expanding human kingdoms pushed nonhuman races into remote regions, sparking repeated elf-human wars, including the slaughter at Loc Muinne and Aelirenn's doomed last stand at Shaerrawedd.

The Order of Witchers was founded to defend humanity from monsters, developing the secretive Trial of the Grasses mutation process whose original creators (possibly Cosimo Malaspina and Alzur) are now lost to history.
Nilfgaard grew from a small southern kingdom into a vast empire through centuries of conquest, eventually bordering the Northern Kingdoms.

Geralt of Rivia was born to the sorceress-druid Vizenna, who abandoned him as an infant at Kaer Morhen; he survived the brutal Trial of the Grasses and additional experimental mutations that left him pale-skinned and white-haired, earning the name 'White Wolf,' with Vesemir becoming his father figure.
As a young witcher, Geralt met Dandelion, who became his lifelong friend and chronicler, romanticizing Geralt's deeds into legend.

In Blaviken, Geralt was caught between sorcerer Stregobor and the cursed bandit Renfri; he killed Renfri and her gang to prevent a massacre, but the ignorant townsfolk branded him the 'Butcher of Blaviken,' a reputation that haunted him and made him warier of interfering in human affairs.

As emperor-in-waiting, young Emhyr var Emreis was cursed into a hedgehog-like form by usurpers and fled toward Cintra seeking a cure, later appearing at Calanthe's court as the mysterious knight Duny/Urcheon of Erlenwald.
At Calanthe's feast in Cintra, Geralt broke Duny's curse and then jokingly invoked the Law of Surprise, unknowingly claiming Pavetta's unborn child—the future Ciri—as his destiny.

Married to Pavetta, Duny (revealed as Emhyr var Emreis) secretly plotted with a mage to fake his family's death in a staged shipwreck to return to Nilfgaard and reclaim the throne; during the crossing Pavetta died and Ciri, protected by her mother's foresight, was left behind.

Ten years after the Cintra feast, Geralt visited to formally renounce his claim on the child, only learning years later that the child was a girl (Ciri) after saving her from a monster in Brokilon Forest.

During these wandering years, Geralt met Yennefer of Vengerberg in Rinde while seeking a cure for Dandelion's cursed throat; he used his final wish from a captured djinn to bind his fate to hers, beginning a stormy, enduring love affair.

Geralt also traveled widely, gaining fame for lifting the curse on Foltest's daughter (a striga), refusing to let Yarpen Zigrin's hunters kill a dragon, and saving witcher Letho of Gulet's life, forging bonds that would matter later.

Emperor Emhyr var Emreis launched the First Nilfgaard War, crushing Cintra at the Marnadal Stairs; Queen Calanthe died in the Slaughter of Cintra rather than be captured, and Ciri became a lost war refugee, while Nilfgaard's advance was finally halted by the Northern coalition at the Second Battle of Sodden, where many sorcerers died defending the Hill of the Fourteen.

Fleeing Cintra's fall, young Ciri survived with druids and a peasant family until Geralt found her again by chance and, recognizing his destiny, took her under his protection, eventually bringing her to the hidden witcher fortress of Kaer Morhen for training and safety.

At Kaer Morhen, Ciri trained in swordplay under Geralt, Vesemir, Eskel and Lambert, forming deep family bonds, and Geralt reconciled his feelings about fatherhood and destiny during this peaceful winter.

Ciri was later sent to Melitele's Temple in Ellander for a broader education, and afterward Geralt arranged for her to continue at Aretuza under Yennefer's protection, deepening Yennefer's role as a maternal figure to her.

Amid rising tensions, Emperor Emhyr promised power to the mage Vilgefortz of Roggeveen in exchange for finding Ciri, while the Lodge of Sorceresses and other factions began scheming for control of her.

The Thanedd Coup erupted at a mage summit on Thanedd Island: Vilgefortz and other traitors, aided by hidden Scoia'tael, attempted to seize Ciri and overthrow the loyalist sorcerers, plunging the Northern mages into civil war and killing many, including exposing Vilgefortz's true allegiance when he defeated Geralt in single combat.

Fleeing the chaos, Ciri stepped through the Tor Lara portal and was flung first to the Korath Desert, then—after surviving with the outlaw Border Rats and later being hunted by the bounty killer Leo Bonhart—into further peril, eventually finding brief refuge with the hermit Vysogota of Corvo.

Gravely wounded after Thanedd, Geralt was rescued by Triss Merigold and healed in Brokilon Forest, then set out with a growing band of companions (Dandelion, Milva, Zoltan, Regis, Cahir, Angouleme) to search for Ciri across war-torn lands.

Meanwhile, Letho of Gulet and fellow Viper School witchers, secretly acting on Nilfgaardian orders, assassinated Kings Demavend and Foltest to destabilize the North, using the Lodge of Sorceresses as a scapegoat.

The Wild Hunt, led by Eredin, began hunting Ciri across worlds for her Elder Blood; to save a captured Yennefer, Geralt traded himself into the Hunt's service, losing his memories in the process, until Ciri devised his rescue roughly a year later.

Geralt, now amnesiac, was found near Kaer Morhen and struggled to rebuild his identity; he investigated the Salamandra syndicate's attack on Kaer Morhen, avenged a slain witcher, and uncovered a plot by Jacques de Aldersberg to breed supermen using stolen witcher secrets before killing him.

Now serving as Foltest's bodyguard, Geralt was later framed for Foltest's assassination and pursued the real killer, discovering it was his former ally Letho of Gulet, who fled into the ongoing war in Aedirn.

Geralt fought at the Yaruga River defending Queen Meve's forces, earning knighthood and the legitimate title 'of Rivia,' then tracked Letho and the Viper witchers into Aedirn's civil war, learning of the Lodge's hand in the regicides before confronting Letho at the Loc Muinne summit, which collapsed into chaos after Nilfgaardian sabotage and a dragon attack.

In the aftermath of Thanedd and the regicides, Yennefer secretly used her own life-force and Ciri's power to transport the wounded Geralt to the mystical Isle of Avallon, healing him outside of time, after which the Wild Hunt tracked and captured her there as bait for Ciri.
Geralt eventually recovered his memories at Loc Muinne, learning Yennefer was alive in Nilfgaard and that Ciri had returned to the world, and later met Emperor Emhyr, who hired him to find her.

Beginning in White Orchard amid the harsh Nilfgaardian occupation of the Third Northern War, Geralt (with Vesemir) resumed his search for Ciri and Yennefer, tracing their path through Velen, Novigrad, and Skellige.

In Velen, Geralt encountered the Bloody Baron and the malevolent Crones of Crookback Bog, learning Ciri had sheltered there before fleeing toward Novigrad; he also discovered the creature Uma, secretly the cursed elf Avallac'h.

In Novigrad, gripped by Eternal Fire persecution of mages and nonhumans, Geralt found and rescued the imprisoned Dandelion, learning Ciri had teleported away after a failed heist against Dijkstra meant to fund Avallac'h's cure.

Reuniting briefly with Yennefer, Geralt was ambushed by the Wild Hunt while traveling to meet Emhyr, then journeyed to Skellige amid its succession crisis, finding evidence of a massive magical battle where Ciri and Avallac'h had fought off the Wild Hunt.

Following the trail to the Isle of Mists, Geralt found Ciri in a magically induced sleep, placed there by Avallac'h for protection; his presence broke the spell and revived her, and together they returned to Kaer Morhen to prepare for the Wild Hunt's final assault.

Gathering allies including Yennefer, Triss, Eskel, Lambert and Letho, Geralt defended Kaer Morhen against Eredin and Imlerith's assault; Vesemir sacrificed his life protecting Ciri, whose grief-fueled Elder Blood power devastated the attackers and forced their retreat.

Rallying the Lodge of Sorceresses, Skellige warriors, and Nilfgaardian forces, Geralt's coalition trapped Eredin's ship the Naglfar in a Skellige bay; Geralt boarded the ghostly vessel and killed Eredin in a climactic duel, who revealed with his dying words that Avallac'h had taken Ciri and deceived them.
With the Wild Hunt broken, Ciri chose to enter the White Frost herself to save the multiverse from encroaching entropy, leaving Geralt to trust in her strength alone.

Depending on the player's choices, the story concludes with one of three fates for Ciri: she fakes her death and becomes a witcher alongside Geralt, she becomes Empress of Nilfgaard, or she fails to return and Geralt is left broken, eventually dying in Velen; in a lighter epilogue Geralt may retire to Corvo Bianco with Yennefer or Triss.
